Article Title: Priscilla Chan's housing philanthropy helped finance 4,400 homes and protect 73,000 tenants in 5 years
Article Text:
Priscilla Chan is the co-founder and co-CEO of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Image Credit: Jessica Chou/Chan Zuckerberg Initiative(CZI)

Priscilla Chan’s philanthropy financed 4,000+ homes and protected over 70,000 tenants

PBF used flexible funding and community-led policy work

What role did Chan Zuckerberg Initiative funding play

Why affordable housing requires more than building new homes

PBF’s 5-year experience is a model to tackle housing challenges

Priscilla Chan with community leaders and CZI staff member Ruby Bolaria-Shifrin celebrating 5 years of the Partnership for the Bay’s Future at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco in March , 2024. Image Credit: Chan Zuckerberg Initiative(CZI)

Priscilla Chan has supported thousands of Bay Area residents through the ‘Partnership for the Bay’s Future,’ a programme created to tackle the region’s shortage of affordable homes. 5 years after its launch, the initiative had protected more than 73,000 tenants and financed over 4,400 homes for thousands of people. The work, supported by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative(CZI) , combines funding with policy support and partnerships involving governments, non-profits, developers and community groups. Its progress shows how philanthropic money can be used alongside other resources to address housing problems.The Partnership for the Bay’s Future(PBF) began in 2019 with a focus on making housing more affordable while supporting racial equity and economic inclusion. According to the CZI’s April 2024 report on the partnership, its first 5 years resulted in more than 73,000 tenants being protected and more than 4,400 homes being financed for 11,000 people.According to the same report, community groups had helped bring the experiences of renters, low-income residents and people of colour into discussions with local, regional and state governments. More than 20,000 community members were engaged through policies connected to this work.The results came through 2 main parts of the partnership. First is policy work and second is housing finance. Instead of relying on a single programme, PBF created different ways to support people who were already living in the region while also helping produce and preserve affordable homes.One part of PBF is its Policy Fund, which provides resources and technical assistance to local and regional governments. The aim is to help officials develop and put into practice policies that can allow more people to remain in their communities.The CZI reported that 36 policies had been proposed through the effort by April 2024, with 13 having passed. Examples included Berkeley’s Preference Policy and Antioch’s Cottage Communities on Faith-Owned Land.CZI reported in May 2024 that California’s housing shortage cannot be addressed through one measure alone and described the need for collaboration between activists, organisers, non-profits, philanthropies, private companies and community members. It also stressed that housing solutions can take time to produce results because the problem has developed over decades.The housing finance side of PBF was designed to help close funding gaps that can prevent affordable housing projects from moving forward. Its ‘Family of Loan Funds’ supports the production and preservation of affordable homes across 5 Bay Area counties.By 2024, the loan funds had raised nearly $600 million and facilitated more than $404 million in investments. Those investments financed more than 4,400 homes. According to CZI, 90% of the units were intended for households earning 80% of the area median income or less, while half were for households at or below 50% of that level.CZI was an early investor, providing $50 million in initial capital. The organisation described that money as low-cost and risk-tolerant funding, which helped bring other funders into the housing effort. The loan funds are managed by the ‘Local Initiatives Support Corporation Bay Area’ and are intended to bridge financing gaps in the region’s rental housing market.CZI also reports about several ways through which California can address affordability. One involves newer construction methods such as modular and panelised building, which can potentially reduce costs and shorten construction times. Another involves alternative forms of ownership, including community land trusts, housing co-operatives and resident-owned communities.The organisation also highlights the importance of protecting homes that are already affordable. Existing lower-cost rental properties can be lost when rents rise or buildings change ownership, leaving residents at risk of displacement. In Los Angeles, for example, CZI highlighted the Local Rental Owners Collaborative, which works with smaller landlords to help preserve housing and keep residents in their homes.Building more homes can increase supply, while preserving existing properties and protecting tenants can address immediate pressures on people already living in expensive areas.The April 2024 announcement described PBF as one of the largest private-sector housing funds focused on the Bay Area’s affordability crisis.At the 5-year mark, the partnership had not only financed thousands of homes but also supported policies affecting tenants across the region.Priscilla Chan has also described philanthropy as a relatively small part of a housing problem of this scale. According to the CZI report, the organisation saw a need for flexible approaches that could add to existing affordable housing support rather than replace it. The PBF reached its fifth anniversary in 2024. Its experience has since been presented as a model that other regions could consider adapting to their own housing challenges.
Article Summary: Priscilla Chan’s philanthropy financed 4,000+ homes and protected over 70,000 tenants. PBF used flexible funding and community-led policy work. Its progress shows how philanthropic money can be used alongside other resources to address housing problems.

Article Title: California shoppers with disabilities say mall skincare stores pressured them into spending thousands; one man says he spent more than $50,000, and a congressman is now seeking state scrutiny
Article Text:
Representative image

Customers with disabilities and older adults said that they were allegedly pressured into spending thousands of dollars at Bee & Co.'s mall-based skincare stores across the Southland, according to CBS California. Now, California congressman Rep. Brad Sherman, whose congressional district includes the Westfield Topanga mall in Canoga Park, said he plans to bring the allegations involving Bee & Co. to the attention of California Attorney General Rob Bonta. "This is not what should be going on in our malls," Sherman said.The investigation developed from a previous story by CBS California Investigates where Victor Chisholm, a man with an intellectual disability, said he spent more than $50,000 during several visits to Bee & Co. last spring. Chisholm told CBS LA that he felt pressured into draining his savings account. When asked if he wanted to spend that amount, Chisholm said, "Uh, no. I did not."Bee & Co. is a skincare and wellness brand that offers natural products and in-store treatments. Since the report about Chisholm was published, other customers have come forward with similar allegations. Gabe Cota, who has a learning disability, said he spent more than $3,000 at Bee & Co.after being drawn into the store by a free sample and a compliment from a saleswoman. "At that point, I was basically in their web, and I couldn't escape until they made a sale," Cota said.Cota said he is slow to process information and that compliments about his appearance can make him feel vulnerable. "Most of my life, I've never really felt attractive," he said. "Part of it is lack of self-confidence." He said the same Bee & Co. salesperson who interacted with Chisholm also persuaded him to make purchases even after he said he did not want to.He said he even locked his debit card to prevent himself from making another purchase but, according to Cota, the salesperson convinced him to send $300 through Zelle. "It makes me angry, it makes me upset, and then it also makes me feel disillusioned because I'm the kind of person who has difficulty saying no to people," Cota said.Chisholm and Cota both alleged that the same salesperson flirted with them and used sales tactics that made them feel pressured to hand over their credit cards.Bee & Co.'s parent company, Mazal Group, is based in Chatsworth. The company recently settled a class-action lawsuit brought by more than 100 customers who alleged unfair and deceptive practices at the company's skincare stores in Hawaii. The customers alleged nearly $1 million in losses.Mazal has denied wrongdoing in connection with the allegations. In a recent email to Chisholm's attorney, Fred Voigtmann, Bee & Co. attorney Efrat Levy said it was Chisholm who engaged in "harassing and inappropriate conduct." Levy also said Bee & Co. "denies any wrongdoing."According to the email, the company offered to return Chisholm's money if he and his attorney removed disparaging comments and online reviews and sent a letter to Westfield stating that Voigtmann "did not know what actually took place between Bee & Co. and its sales representatives and Mr Chisholm."Westfield, which operates the Topanga mall, said in an email that the "reported treatment of this customer is deeply troubling" and that it was "evaluating appropriate legal remedies."According to Sherman, the allegations could create problems for the mall. "This is a reputational risk, perhaps even a legal risk for the mall," he said.The allegations are not limited to Bee & Co. In 2024, a Mazal-affiliated store called Lionesse at Westfield Fashion Square in Sherman Oaks settled a lawsuit with a woman in her 70s who accused the business of elder abuse and deceptive sales practices.Two women, both now in their 80s, also told the station they were pressured into buying expensive skincare products at Mazal-affiliated stores at the Shops at Santa Anita. Both took their cases to small claims court, where they reached settlements. The mall declined to comment, saying the matter involved an "independently operated tenant."Simon, which owns Del Amo Fashion Centre, was also contacted repeatedly for comment but did not respond.The allegations against the retailers have not been adjudicated in court, and the companies have denied wrongdoing in connection with the claims. Chisolm's attorney has created a website where people can report their experiences with coercive skincare sales.
Article Summary: Customers with disabilities and older adults said that they were allegedly pressured into spending thousands of dollars at Bee & Co.'s mall-based skincare stores across the Southland. California congressman Rep. Brad Sherman said he plans to bring the allegations to the attention of California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

Article Title: Kristin Cavallari bought a secluded 130-acre Tennessee estate in 2024 and spent two years reshaping it, turning a barn into an indoor basketball court and a guesthouse into her podcast studio
Article Text:
The result is a home that combines expansive surroundings with a surprisingly practical approach to family life, giving Cavallari the privacy of a secluded estate without sacrificing the comforts of a house designed for everyday living.

A new chapter outside Nashville

A familiar design language

Creating a quieter retreat

For Kristin Cavallari, the appeal of her new Tennessee home goes well beyond its size. Tucked away on 130 acres outside Nashville, the secluded estate has become a private base for family life, work and the slower pace she wanted after moving on from her former Nashville property. The reality television veteran was not actively house hunting when a real estate agent friend encouraged her to visit the one-story residence in 2024. The combination of privacy, expansive land and floor-to-ceiling windows quickly changed that. What followed was a two-year transformation focused less on dramatic decoration and more on making the property work around her life and her three children, states an online report by Realtor.As per the report, Cavallari had been looking for a fresh start after selling the Nashville home she had once shared with former NFL quarterback Jay Cutler. The former couple, who split in 2020, finalized their divorce in 2022 and sold their shared mansion for $3.7 million in 2020, considerably below its $5.3 million purchase price in 2012 and its later $7.9 million asking price.Cavallari also purchased another Nashville property for $3 million around the time she and Cutler announced their separation.Her current estate, however, offered something those homes could not: expansive acreage and a much greater degree of privacy, adds the report. She shares the Tennessee property with sons Camden, 14, and Jaxon, 12, and daughter Saylor, 10.According to Architectural Digest, for the interiors, Cavallari again worked with longtime friend and interior designer April Tomlin. The pair had previously created a calm, grounding aesthetic in Cavallari's former home, using neutral tones, bright white interiors and understated furnishings. That visual language carried into the new residence. Surprisingly little needed to be changed, with Cavallari bringing much of her existing furniture into the property. Even many of the home's original details, including its light fixtures, remained. Tomlin's approach centered on a no-fuss environment that could still feel warm and comfortable, with muted and earthy tones providing much of the visual character.Turning the property into a one-stop homeThe Architectural Digest report adds that the biggest transformation was functional. Because of the estate's remote location, Cavallari wanted to reduce the amount of time spent driving back and forth for everyday activities. A home gym eliminated a roughly 25-minute drive each way, while a new bathtub and a substantially larger closet added practical upgrades inside the main house. The expanded closet also became part of the home's design, with Cavallari's clothing collection influencing the space.The barn was converted into an indoor basketball court for her sons, giving the boys a dedicated space to play without leaving the property. The guesthouse took on a professional role, becoming a recording studio for Cavallari's Let's Be Honest podcast, which has secured a seven-figure deal with Dear Media.The report adds that a new pool completed the outdoor transformation. Designed by Basin Pool Designs owner Nick Buchholz, the pool was conceived to create a sense of calm while visually connecting with the house rather than feeling like a separate feature. After two years of changes, the estate has evolved into more than a large rural property. Its design, amenities and layout have been carefully shaped around Cavallari's daily routine and her children's interests.The result is a home that combines expansive surroundings with a surprisingly practical approach to family life, giving Cavallari the privacy of a secluded estate without sacrificing the comforts of a house designed for everyday living.Images Courtesy: instagram and Architectural Digest
Article Summary: Kristin Cavallari bought the 130-acre estate outside Nashville in 2024. The reality television veteran had been looking for a fresh start after selling the Nashville home she had once shared with former NFL quarterback Jay Cutler. She shares the Tennessee property with sons Camden, 14, and Jaxon, 12, and daughter Saylor, 10. For the interiors, she worked with longtime friend and interior designer April Tomlin.

Article Title: An Alabama couple bought 21 acres in Jackson Hole in the 1990s; decades later, their family retreat is asking $40 million
Article Text:
PC: LATHAM JENKINS/ The Wall Street Journal

How did the Rotenstreichs expand their Jackson Hole retreat

What natural features and Western-style interiors define the Jackson Hole retreat

PC: LATHAM JENKINS/ The Wall Street Journal

Why are the Rotenstreichs selling their $40 million Jackson Hole property

An Alabama couple who bought a 21-acre property in Jackson Hole in the 1990s has spent decades turning it into a family retreat with a Western-style lodge, guest cottage and creek and riverfront grounds. Investor Jon Rotenstreich and his wife, Susan, initially lived in the two-bedroom guest cottage while renovating and expanding the main house to about 5,900 square feet. The compound also includes a 1,730-square-foot barn, an art studio, a teepee and a section of the Snake River. Now, after years of summers, holidays and family visits, the Rotenstreichs are listing the property for $40 million.After purchasing the property, the Rotenstreichs initially lived in the two-bedroom guest cottage while renovating the main house. According to The Wall Street Journal, they expanded the main house to about 5,900 square feet. Details were added throughout the home, including a main staircase with a handrail made by a woodworker who measured Susan’s hand to customise the size of the grip.The property also includes a garage with an art studio, where Susan, a former jewellery designer trained as an energy healer, liked to paint. A 1,730-square-foot barn contains a workshop, while a teepee is also located on the grounds.The couple’s grandchildren have slept in the teepee, and the family has used the area for campfires, songs and roasting marshmallows and s’mores.The Jackson Hole compound includes both the creek and a section of the Snake River. A small island in the middle of the Snake River provides habitat for moose, elk and deer. Susan Rotenstreich said the family can snowshoe there during winter. The property also has a kitchen garden outside the main house, enclosed by a fence made from woven willow branches.The interiors were also developed in a Western style, with the Rotenstreichs using local craftsmen during the renovation. A local blacksmith handmade all of the fireplace tools, while a carpenter made furniture and decorative birch cabinets. The guest cottage includes a bookcase made from half of an old canoe, and the furniture in the home is included in the asking price.The Rotenstreichs are now selling the Jackson Hole property for $40 million. The compound includes a six-bedroom main house and a two-bedroom guest cottage. The couple declined to disclose how much they originally paid for the property, with the Journal noting that Wyoming is a nondisclosure state.The couple said they are selling because they feel it is time to downsize, although they still plan to visit Jackson Hole. The property is in the Ely Springs subdivision near Jackson. Listing agent Latham Jenkins of Live Water Properties told the Journal that real-estate values in the area have risen sharply since COVID and said the top end of the market continues to see demand.
Article Summary: Jon and Susan Rotenstreich bought a 21-acre property in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, in the 1990s and have spent decades turning it into a family retreat. The compound includes a six-bedroom main house, a two-bedroom guest cottage, a 1,730-square-foot barn, an art studio, a teepee and a section of the Snake River. The couple are now selling the property for $40 million.

Article Title: How China helped arm Iran before Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi
Article Text:
File photo: Chinese president Xi Jinping and US president Donald Trump

The supply line to Iran

China's oil lifeline; and Washington's dilemma

The satellite trail

Contradiction at the heart of the Xi-Trump summit

US president Donald Trump hosted a grand welcome for Chinese president Xi Jinping but in the background of this fanfare, an investigation by the Wall Street Journal has shown how China has been supporting Iran militarily in its war against the US.When the US and Iran agreed to a temporary truce this summer, China was quick to highlight its diplomatic role.Beijing said its foreign ministry had made dozens of calls to help ease tensions, while Xi Jinping had personally offered suggestions aimed at ending the conflict.But on the very day the truce was signed, a Chinese aircraft landed in Tehran carrying electronics for Iran’s ministry of defense. According to Iranian customs records analysed by WSJ, some of the components could be used in drone systems and missile guidance equipment.This shipment was also not an isolated incident, as WSJ found records of around 1,300 shipments of dual-use components from China to Iran’s defence ministry through the end of June. Two days after the truce-day delivery, more than a dozen additional shipments arrived carrying parts worth over $6 million that could be used in drones.With Xi currently in Washington for talks with Trump, China's relationship with Iran has emerged as an uncomfortable issue sitting beneath the official summit agenda of trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan.WSJ’s investigation, based on Iranian customs records, US officials and people familiar with the transactions, describes a growing air bridge between China and Iran.Records covering January 2025 through June 2026 show thousands of shipments to Iran's defence ministry and Iranian companies. They included GPS tracking equipment, electric motors and aircraft-engine components. Many shipments carried references to Article 119 of Iranian customs regulations, which provides tariff exemptions for defence imports.The flow intensified after the US Navy restricted Iranian maritime trade.Iranian airline Mahan Air, which is under US sanctions, increased flights from Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou to Tehran from four a week in early March to about 27 a week by late April, according to FlightRadar24 data.By the first week of September, Mahan Air had flown 39 times from China to Iran, roughly twice its prewar level. Many of those flights appeared to be focused on cargo rather than passengers, WSJ reported.Researchers tracking Iranian trade told WSJ that some of the Chinese suppliers involved are little-known companies working with Iranian importers.Kate Koren, deputy director of the economics programme at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told WSJ that some of the components being traded are known to be used in Iran's Shahed drones. A forthcoming CSIS report, she said, identified Chinese companies publicly advertising sensitive electronics this year.The report also stated that Chinese companies have supplied Iran with chemical materials including sodium perchlorate, which can be used to make propellant for ballistic missiles. US authorities have also sanctioned Chinese and Hong Kong-based companies over alleged efforts to help Iran acquire weapons and military equipment.In one case, US officials said a procurement network tried to obtain Chinese shoulder-fired missile systems for Iran and route them through Belarus to conceal the Iranian end-user. The attempted transaction was unsuccessful, according to those officials.The relationship is not one-sided but rather symbiotic.China has become Iran's largest oil customer, providing Tehran with a major source of revenue despite US sanctions. Chinese front companies and financial networks have helped facilitate Iranian oil transactions and move money through China's financial system.Iran and China deepened their relationship after the Trump administration's 2018 "maximum pressure" campaign. The two countries signed a 25-year strategic cooperation pact in 2021, while China became the dominant buyer of Iranian crude.US lawmakers have said China buys more than 80% of Iran's crude exports. More recently, a US Senate foreign relations committee statement citing Treasury figures put the share at about 90%.Washington has responded with hundreds of sanctions against Iranian and Chinese entities since the war began, including companies accused of helping Tehran obtain weapons, components or revenue.Yet the Trump administration has so far been cautious about directly confronting Beijing, especially after the earlier tariff confrontation exposed China’s leverage.People familiar with discussions inside the administration told WSj that Trump had made maintaining good relations with Xi a priority ahead of the summit. Some senior officials have consequently played down the significance of Chinese assistance to Iran.That approach has created disagreement within Washington, with defence secretary Pete Hegseth blaming China for enabling Iran, a claim Trump rejected stating, “I trust them.”According to US officials cited by WSJ, Iran used satellite imagery obtained from Chinese entities before and after a July 17 strike that killed three US troops.The Trump administration had already sanctioned three Chinese satellite-imagery companies in May, saying the companies had provided information that could help Iran target US forces.That has intensified pressure within Washington to confront Beijing.In late August, Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent launched "Operation Economic Outcast", aimed at cutting the economic networks sustaining Iran. The US subsequently sanctioned a China-owned oil tanker and Chinese companies and individuals accused of helping Iran obtain critical components.But the administration did not impose major new sanctions directly on Chinese financial institutions.Meanwhile, Iranian oil has continued reaching China.Kpler estimated that around four million barrels were delivered to China in the week after Operation Economic Outcast began.And despite sanctions and the wider conflict, Mahan Air continues to fly to China.Xi’s arrival in Washington now carries two very different messages.China wants to be seen as a country capable of brokering peace and stabilising the Middle East. Beijing has publicly rejected attempts to associate it with the conflict and says it opposes unilateral US sanctions and supports diplomatic efforts to end the fighting.At the same time, WSJ’s investigation found evidence of continued Chinese trade with Iran involving components that can have military applications.Chinese officials have said Beijing strictly regulates exports of dual-use goods and rejects allegations that it is deliberately supporting the conflict.The tension is therefore not simply about whether China supports Iran. It is about how far Beijing is willing to go, and how far Washington is willing to push back, while both sides try to preserve a broader relationship.The same China that Trump wants to keep close for trade and strategic reasons is deeply embedded in the economic and supply networks helping Iran sustain itself.And that makes Iran an awkward third presence at a summit ostensibly about America and China.
Article Summary: Investigation by the Wall Street Journal shows how China has been supporting Iran militarily in its war against the US. When the US and Iran agreed to a temporary truce this summer, China was quick to highlight its diplomatic role. On the very day the truce was signed, a Chinese aircraft landed in Tehran carrying electronics for Iran’s ministry of defense.

Article Title: Rikishi had spent everything on his new Florida home when Yokozuna gave him a blank cheque to fix its broken heating system
Article Text:
PC: WWE

Rikishi’s early WWF career came with a much smaller payday

Yokozuna gave Rikishi a blank cheque when his family needed help

Yokozuna’s WWF success brought opportunities Rikishi had yet to reach

The blank cheque became a story Rikishi carried with him

Yokozuna’s relationship with Rikishi’s family went beyond wrestling

From Junior Fatu to Rikishi

Before Rikishi became one of WWE ’s recognisable stars, there was a period when simply keeping his new family home running had become a financial problem. According to the various online reports, he had put almost everything he had into a Florida property while wrestling as Fatu, leaving little money for an essential repair. At the same time, his cousin Rodney Anoa’i was enjoying a very different level of success as Yokozuna, having risen to the top of the WWF and become one of its biggest earners. When Rikishi found himself unable to afford a new heating system, Anoa’i offered help in a way that Rikishi would remember for decades.Rikishi, whose real name is Solofa Fatu Jr., was already working in the WWF when his cousin Rodney Anoa’i was becoming a major attraction under the Yokozuna name. The two were members of the same wider wrestling family, but their positions on the roster and their earnings were far apart.Fatu was performing as one half of The Headshrinkers alongside Samu, while Yokozuna had moved into championship programmes and main-event matches. According to ITR Wrestling, by 1993, Yokozuna had become WWF Champion, putting him in a financial position that was very different from that of several relatives still working lower down the card.For Rikishi, the difference became particularly apparent after he moved his family into a new Florida home. He later recalled that he had put virtually everything he had into the property. There was a house, there were children to look after, but there was also a problem that could not simply be left alone.The expense came at an awkward time. After paying for the home, Rikishi said he had nothing available to deal with the heating system. It was not a question of choosing between two home improvements or delaying a renovation. His account was that his family needed a functioning system and he did not have the money to install one.That was when Yokozuna stepped in. Rikishi later described his cousin not by his wrestling identity but by his given name, Rodney Anoa'i. According to his recollection, Anoa'i handed him a blank cheque, already signed, allowing him to use whatever amount was necessary to get the heating installed.The gesture meant that the family could stay in the house with working heat rather than having Rikishi try to find money he did not have.The circumstances made sense within the rapidly changing fortunes of the Anoa'i and Fatu wrestling families. Yokozuna had arrived in the WWF as a huge physical presence managed by Mr Fuji and quickly moved towards the top of the promotion.His breakthrough came at WrestleMania IX, where he defeated Bret Hart for the WWF Championship. Although Hulk Hogan took the title from him almost immediately afterwards, Yokozuna returned to the championship picture later that year.He won the WWF Championship again at the King of the Ring in June 1993, before eventually losing it to Hart at WrestleMania X the following year. Those high-profile programmes came with a level of income that was not available to every member of the family working in wrestling. Rikishi's career was progressing too, but he was still competing in a very different part of the WWF card.The contrast was particularly important when his personal finances became stretched.Rikishi spoke about the incident years later for the WWE Icons documentary focused on Yokozuna. By then, he had established himself as a major WWF and WWE performer in his own right and had become the father of Jimmy and Jey Uso.Looking back, he connected the episode to the way he remembered Yokozuna treating their wider family. In his telling, the money was not offered as a loan or presented as a business arrangement. It was simply help when a relative needed it.That distinction mattered to Rikishi. In an interview with WWE , he remembered the person behind the Yokozuna character, describing how Rodney Anoa'i had been there for him during a difficult period rather than presenting the story simply as something done by a wealthy wrestling star. The heating system was the immediate reason for the cheque. The memory, however, was tied to a much larger family relationship.Rikishi's recollections were also supported by memories shared by his son Jey Uso in the same documentary. Jey described Yokozuna visiting the family home and being treated as an uncle rather than as a major wrestling celebrity.According to Wrestling.Inc,“He would come over to the house, my dad would always be like, 'Hey Uncle Rodney's (Yokozuna) coming through, you know, make sure you make his bed," Jey Uso said. "'Always bring him coffee.' That's a hundred dollars. Hey, he would give us a hundred."There was a practical side to those visits. Jey recalled being told to make sure Yokozuna had his bed ready and to bring him coffee. He also remembered Yokozuna giving the children money when he visited.Those details provide a different picture of the relationship from the one seen on WWF television. On screen, Yokozuna was presented as an imposing champion and one of the promotion's biggest stars. At home, the family relationship came first.For Rikishi, that distinction was particularly clear during the period when he was struggling financially.At the time of the heating incident, Rikishi was still known to wrestling audiences primarily as Fatu. His eventual transformation into Rikishi came later, after years spent working in tag teams and under different characters.His career would eventually take him into the WWF Intercontinental Championship picture, major storylines and a prominent place in the next generation of the Anoa'i family's wrestling legacy.Yokozuna's career followed a much shorter path. Born Rodney Agatupu Anoa'i, he became a two-time WWF Champion and one of the defining heavyweight performers of the early 1990s. His career was cut short by his death in 2000 at the age of 34.
Article Summary: Yokozuna gave Rikishi a blank cheque when his family needed help. Rikishi had put almost everything he had into a Florida property while wrestling as Fatu. At the same time, his cousin Rodney Anoa’i was enjoying a different level of success as Yokozuna.

Article Title: Engineers dredged 500,000 cubic yards of sand from the Mississippi River and used it to build seven islands; six years later, the $25 million McGregor Lake project has restored 270 acres of aquatic ha
Article Text:
Sand dredged from the river becomes new habitat

Seven islands, rock structures and shoreline work

Why McGregor Lake needed intervention

A six-year restoration project

For years, sand dredged from the Mississippi River was removed to keep one of America's most important waterways navigable. At one restoration site, engineers found another use for that material, building islands. The US Army Corps of Engineers has completed a $25 million habitat restoration project at McGregor Lake in Wisconsin, where about 500,000 cubic yards of clean sand dredged from the Mississippi River were used to construct seven islands.The project, which began in 2020, has now improved more than 270 acres of aquatic habitat while also restoring floodplain forest and protecting wetlands.McGregor Lake is a 200-acre backwater lake located in Pool 10 of the Mississippi River near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin. It lies within the Upper Mississippi River National Wildlife and Fish Refuge, an area that supports a wide range of aquatic and terrestrial wildlife. The completed project was marked by the US Army Corps of Engineers' St Paul District on September 22, following six years of restoration work.The project brought together two needs that might otherwise have been treated separately: maintaining the Mississippi River's navigation channel and restoring habitat in one of its backwater lakes.Dredging is routinely carried out in the river to maintain navigation. At McGregor Lake, engineers reused approximately 500,000 cubic yards of clean river sand generated through that process to create seven islands.The islands were not simply piles of dredged material. They were designed as part of a larger habitat restoration effort, with material from additional dredging placed on top to provide suitable ground for vegetation.Engineers also dredged 35 acres of backwater fisheries habitat. The deeper areas created through this work provide overwintering habitat for fish, while the dredged material was reused on the islands.The result was a project in which material removed to maintain the river's navigation channel was redirected into a new landscape intended to support wildlife.The seven newly constructed islands are one of several components of the restoration. The Corps also built five rock features and stabilised more than one mile of shoreline. These measures were designed to reduce erosion and protect aquatic and terrestrial habitat around the lake.According to the Corps, the overall project improved more than 270 acres of aquatic habitat, enhanced more than 45 acres of floodplain forest and protected 22 acres of wetlands. The work was particularly focused on improving conditions for backwater fish species and encouraging the growth of both emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation.McGregor Lake's location within the Mississippi River floodplain makes these habitats important beyond the lake itself. The surrounding river corridor supports migrating songbirds as well as nesting bald eagles, herons, kingfishers and other bird species.Backwater areas such as McGregor Lake are important components of the Upper Mississippi River ecosystem. They provide comparatively sheltered environments where fish can feed, reproduce and survive seasonal conditions. Over time, however, erosion and changes in the lake's habitat can reduce the quality and variety of these environments.The restoration project was designed to address several of those problems at once. Increasing aquatic vegetation provides additional cover and habitat for fish and other wildlife, while the new islands and floodplain forest areas create additional terrestrial habitat. Shoreline stabilisation is also intended to limit erosion that can otherwise degrade habitat and alter the shape and depth of backwater areas.The Corps said the project was designed to increase the age and species diversity of self-sustaining floodplain forests while protecting aquatic and terrestrial habitat by reducing erosion.Construction began in 2020 and continued through 2026, with the project now reaching completion after six years. The work was carried out as part of the Upper Mississippi River Restoration programme, a federal initiative focused on improving habitat and monitoring resources along the river.The programme has been operating for four decades and has completed more than 62 habitat projects benefiting approximately 120,000 acres between Minneapolis and St Louis, according to the Corps.McGregor Lake is therefore part of a much larger effort to balance the Mississippi River's role as a major transportation route with the ecological needs of its surrounding wetlands, backwaters and forests.
Article Summary: US Army Corps of Engineers has completed a $25 million habitat restoration project at McGregor Lake in Wisconsin. About 500,000 cubic yards of clean sand dredged from the Mississippi River were used to construct seven islands. The project has improved more than 270 acres of aquatic habitat while also restoring floodplain forest and protecting wetlands.

Article Title: At 10, Michael Kearney became the world’s youngest university graduate; he had entered college at six
Article Text:
Michael Kearney became the world’s youngest university graduate at 10

How Kearney’s family adapted education to his pace

Kearney’s ambitions moved beyond education and into television

Kearney traded university life for a day as junior mayor

Anthropology was only the beginning

A childhood that did not follow the usual timetable

At an age when most children are still several years away from secondary school, Michael Kearney was already preparing for life after university. As reported by Guinness World Records, in June 1994, at just 10 years and four months old, the American became the youngest person recorded by Guinness World Records to graduate from a university, earning a bachelor’s degree in anthropology from the University of South Alabama. His childhood had followed an unusual route from the beginning. He learned to read at eight months, joined Mensa at four and entered junior college at six after completing his high school studies through home education. By the time he became a graduate, his family was already planning what might come next.Kearney's graduation in 1994 was the point at which an unusual childhood became a documented academic record. He received his BA in anthropology from the University of South Alabama in Mobile, completing a degree normally associated with students many years older.The achievement attracted considerable attention in the United States, although the interest did not last. Rather than treating the degree as the end of his academic career, Kearney was already looking towards postgraduate study.The signs that Kearney was progressing unusually quickly had appeared when he was still an infant. His parents recalled him asking about dinner when he was only four months old. At eight months, he had begun reading.According to the Los Angeles Times, by 4, he had joined Mensa, whose membership is reserved for people who score within the top 2% of the population on approved intelligence tests. Two years later, he had completed a high school certificate through home study and entered Santa Rosa Junior College.The family's approach was highly involved. His mother, Cassidy Kearney, had training as a teacher and took primary responsibility for his education through high school and into college. She prepared herself for the material he was studying, sometimes working through textbooks ahead of his classes so that the formal lessons became largely a period of revision for him.It was an arrangement that demanded time from both parents. Michael's father, Kevin Kearney, left the US Navy.Conventional schooling had not always suited Kearney. His family described difficult encounters with schools and professionals in Alabama and California, with different assessments made about his behaviour and learning needs.His father later argued that Michael was being mistaken for a child who struggled to pay attention when the problem was almost the opposite. He absorbed material rapidly and needed something sufficiently demanding to occupy him.The family eventually developed its own educational system around that fact. Books, home lessons and computers became part of everyday life. Computers, Cassidy said, had become essential to managing the demands of teaching a child who moved through material so quickly.His younger sister, Maeghan, was also being educated at home. She was nine at the time of the 1995 report, although she planned to wait until she was older before entering college.Kearney's unusual education received a particularly warm response in Japan, where he became a recognisable figure and attracted interest from companies considering endorsement opportunities. A book about Michael and his family was also due to be published there.The family's connection with Japan was partly linked to Cassidy's Japanese-American background, but the attention went beyond that. Kevin Kearney contrasted the response with the family's experiences in American education, where Michael's abilities had sometimes created difficulties rather than opening doors. The difference became especially apparent when the family began exploring opportunities outside education.Kearney was interested in television and wanted to become a game show host. For a child who had already completed university, the ambition was not simply something his parents dismissed as a childhood fantasy. He had undergone auditions, attended job interviews and appeared in a television production.One quiz show audition produced an unexpected problem. According to the account published at the time, some adult participants were uncomfortable when the young host corrected their mistakes.His age was unusual enough. His measured IQ, reported as being close to 200, added another layer to the situation, as reported by Los Angeles Times.Kearney's television ambitions gave him an unusual outlet for the same quickness that had shaped his education. He was comfortable with computers and games, and he had already become a fan of The Price Is Right as a young child.His interest in game shows eventually led to a more unusual public appearance. After defeating Santa Barbara mayor Hal Conklin in the computer game SimCity during a national television programme, Kearney was invited to serve as the city's junior mayor for a day.He took part in the day's official activities, including inspections, press events and a City Council meeting. His assessment of the experience was characteristically brief: listening to citizens was the least enjoyable part, while issuing proclamations was more appealing.Among his honorary proclamations was a letter recognising Bill Gates, then chairman of Microsoft, for his contribution to the spread of computers and computer games. For a 10-year-old who had already completed university, the appearance was another example of how far removed his daily life was from that of most children his age.Although television attracted Kearney's attention, his academic path continued. His first degree was in anthropology, but he did not remain confined to that field. According to Guinness World Records, in January 1996, he began classes at Middle Tennessee State University. Later that year, he was admitted to its chemistry programme, beginning another shift in his academic interests.By then, his education was moving into the sciences. On August 9, 1998, at 14 years and eight months old, Kearney received a Master of Science degree in biochemistry. He graduated with an A-minus grade-point average.The master's degree meant that the 10-year-old university graduate of 1994 had, within four years, moved from an undergraduate degree in anthropology to postgraduate work in biochemistry. His academic record had continued to develop even as the public attention surrounding his childhood achievement had faded.Kearney's early years were shaped less by a conventional school progression than by the pace at which he could absorb new material. His parents responded by building an education around him, rather than expecting him to remain within the age-based structure of ordinary schooling.That approach came with practical costs. His mother devoted years to teaching and accompanying him through college work. His father altered his career to spend more time with the family. Computers became an important educational tool, and the household eventually moved between locations as Michael's opportunities developed. By the mid-1990s, the family was preparing to move from the Universal City area to Burbank, with trips to Japan also part of their lives.The question was no longer whether a 10-year-old could graduate from university. Michael Kearney had already done that.
Article Summary: Michael Kearney became the world's youngest university graduate in 1994. He learned to read at eight months, joined Mensa at four and entered junior college at six after completing his high school studies through home education. By the time he became a graduate, his family was already planning what might come next. Kearney was interested in television and wanted to become a game show host. He had undergone auditions, attended job interviews and appeared in a television production.

Article Title: Pakistan appoints former army general Nauman Mahmood as first head of Mecca alliance
Article Text:
The Mecca defence pact was signed on August 7

Pakistan on Wednesday appointed a former Pakistan Army officer as the first secretary-general of the country's trilateral Mecca pact with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia Lieutenant general Nauman Mahmood (retired) will head the alliance’s general secretariat, which is being established in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.“The government of Pakistan is pleased to announce the appointment of Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood, Hilal-i-Imtiaz (Military), (retired), as the first secretary general pursuant to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office said in a statement.Mahmood, who served in the military’s Baloch Regiment, previously commanded a key Pakistan Army corps in the country’s restive northwest and also served as president of the National Defence University in Islamabad.His appointment comes amid an escalation involving Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, the Yemeni rebels who have carried out attacks on Saudi territory in recent days and established control over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye signed the Mecca pact on August 7.Modelled on Nato’s Article 5, the agreement establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one member would be regarded as an attack against all three.The alliance held its inaugural meeting on August 31 in Istanbul, Türkiye, where officials from the three member states met to establish its institutional structure. They decided that the first secretary-general would be from Pakistan, paving the way for Mahmood’s appointment.
Article Summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye signed the Mecca pact on August 7. The agreement establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one member would be regarded as an attack against all three. Lieutenant general Nauman Mahmood (retired) will head the alliance’s general secretariat.

Article Title: A 67-year-old Idaho teacher retired and drove across the US to Delaware after her daughter's daycare bill matched the mortgage; she now provides about 30 hours of childcare every week for her granddau
Article Text:
Mary Jo Galusha now spends about 30 hours each week caring for her granddaughter (NPR photo)

Rising costs push families to grandparents

Millions of grandparents provide regular care

Sacrifice for grandparents

Galusha plans to care until kindergarten

A 67-year-old retired schoolteacher from Idaho moved across the US to Delaware after her daughter decided to have a second child despite the high cost of childcare. Mary Jo Galusha retired from teaching and drove cross-country in her red Volkswagen Beetle to help her daughter, Stacia Bourne, and her family, WTJX NewsFeed reported.Bourne, a University of Delaware psychology professor who lives in Maryland, and her husband had been worried about the cost of raising another child. Their first child, George, was born in 2020 and started daycare at the age of two. "The cost for childcare for him is about the same as our mortgage," Bourne said.The couple had been discussing whether they could afford a second child when Galusha offered to help. She told her daughter that if they decided to have another baby, she would retire and move from Idaho to the East Coast to provide childcare.Several months later, Galusha received the call that Bourne was expecting. "I got a call that Stacia was expecting and that I better start planning on retiring," Galusha recalled with a laugh. She then retired from her job as a schoolteacher, packed her belongings and made the long drive to Delaware.Galusha, who is now the grandmother of five, lives in Newark, Delaware. Her granddaughter Robin was born in late 2024 and spends about 30 hours a week in Galusha's care while her parents work.Galusha has also replaced her Volkswagen Beetle with an SUV so that two car seats can fit more easily in the back row. "It's a joy," Galusha said. "It's like magic to watch them grow up."Galusha's decision comes as more families in the US are relying on grandparents for childcare. Grandparents have always helped look after grandchildren, but rising childcare costs have made that support more important for families who cannot easily afford daycare.According to Child Care Aware of America, the average annual cost of childcare for children under five in the US was $13,184 in 2025. In some cases, childcare costs can be close to the cost of rent or college tuition.Nicole Jorwic, chief programme officer at Caring Across Generations, said families are turning to older relatives because of gaps in the childcare system."The reality is that because this country hasn't invested in a childcare infrastructure that is flexible and affordable and reliable, grandparents are filling in the gaps that the service system leaves behind," she said.Madonna Harrington Meyer, a Syracuse University sociology professor who studies ageing and grandparenting, said several factors have increased the need for childcare. More households now have both parents working full-time, while the number of single mothers has also increased over the decades.Families raising children with disabilities can face another challenge because they may need childcare providers who can offer specialised care. "All of these things are reasons people turn to grandparents," Harrington Meyer said.Galusha is one of millions of grandparents who help care for grandchildren. One poll found that nearly half of respondents with grandchildren under 18 looked after them at least once every few months.An AARP report from June found that the main reasons grandparents provide childcare include parents being busy or working and grandparents wanting to spend time with their grandchildren.The median amount of time grandparents spent caring for grandchildren, excluding those who are primary caregivers or provide no care, was 200 hours a year, or about 3.8 hours a week, according to the data.Having grandparents provide childcare can also offer greater flexibility than formal daycare. Harrington Meyer said grandparents may care for children at their own homes or at the children's homes and can adjust arrangements around the family's needs."They are so flexible," Harrington Meyer said. "Unlike a formal daycare situation, often grandparents will come to your house, or they'll alternate between watching the children at their own house and at the grandparent's house."Grandparents can also benefit from spending time with their grandchildren. One study found higher scores on memory and verbal fluency tests among grandparents who provided care.However, regular childcare can be demanding, especially for older people who have already raised their own children. It can affect their health, social lives and careers. Grandparents who move closer to their grandchildren may also have to leave behind friends and familiar surroundings.Jerry Larkin, 66, a former machinist, moved in with his daughter's family in Tulsa, Oklahoma, during the Covid-19 pandemic to help care for his twin grandsons. One of the children requires additional medical care."Being raised in the '60s, there were a lot of stay-at-home moms and everything, so this wasn't really a thing," Larkin said. "But now that everybody's got to work two jobs, it's become a thing."Yalanda Lattimore, 59, also provides regular care for her one-year-old granddaughter, Mavee. She looks after her for one and a half days each week. Lattimore said the arrangement has reduced the time she can spend on her handmade soap business and media work."I felt like I could make the sacrifice more than they could, and it truly has been a sacrifice," she said. "You just put things on hold, because your priorities are different."For Galusha, her pension from her years as a schoolteacher in Idaho makes it possible to provide unpaid childcare after retirement. Her home in Newark has a bedroom for her grandchildren, a playroom filled with Legos and a crafting area for George.Galusha and Bourne use a shared Google Calendar to organise the children's care. The current plan is for Galusha to look after Robin until she starts kindergarten, although the two review the arrangement every six months.Bourne said having her mother provide the care gives the family a sense of security, but there is little backup if the arrangement changes."I'd much prefer to have my mom take care of Robin, but then you always worry, like if in six months she decides that she wants to move and be near another grandbaby, then we'll have to scramble and figure out something else," Bourne said. Galusha responded from across the table, "No plans for that."For Lattimore, the time spent caring for her granddaughter is also about being present for her family. "What you really want is somebody to say you were there, that you were there for them," she said. "Those are the memories that I want."She said parents should not have to choose between paying for childcare and giving up work. After raising four children herself, she wanted her daughter to have a different experience."When my daughter got ready to start her family, I just didn't want her to go through that," Lattimore said. "I wanted her to have the balance. If work-life balance exists for somebody, I wanted it for my daughter," she added. For families like Bourne’s, that support can mean more than saving on childcare; it can also give grandparents a meaningful role in the everyday lives of the next generation.
Article Summary: Millions of grandparents provide regular care for their grandchildren. Mary Jo Galusha, 67, moved from Idaho to Delaware to care for her granddaughter. Galusha's decision comes as more families in the US are relying on grandparents for childcare. Average annual cost of childcare for children under five in US was $13,184 in 2025.

Article Title: An Oklahoma man says he bought five acres from his grandfather in 1994; 32 years later, the county says it owns a 40-foot strip inches from his house and plans to auction it with a $29,000 starting bi
Article Text:
Image Credit: news9.com.

A thirty-two-year land ownership surprise

Structural proximity and access concerns

Public meetings and local government response

An Oklahoma homeowner who bought five acres of land from his grandfather in 1994 has learned that local authorities claim ownership of a narrow strip of land right next to his house, which is now set to be sold at a public tax auction. Thirty-two years after buying the rural property, the homeowner was told by Oklahoma County officials that a 40-foot strip of land just inches from his front door technically belongs to the county. Local authorities plan to put the disputed piece of land up for auction, with bidding set to start at $29,000. According to an investigation published by AOL News, the dispute centers on a long-standing boundary mistake that went unnoticed for more than three decades, despite multiple tax assessments and property reviews.The homeowner originally bought the five-acre plot from his grandfather in 1994, believing the sale covered the full area around his family home. For 32 years, he mowed the yard, paid property taxes, and lived on the land without ever hearing about any boundary dispute from local government. The issue came up recently when Oklahoma County officials reviewed regional land records and found an unassigned, tax-delinquent strip measuring 40 feet wide right along his house.County records published online through DocketCity, which covers Oklahoma County public meetings, show that the land in question was flagged during a routine review of county-held property and unpaid tax rolls. The county then listed the narrow strip of land for public auction to recover unpaid taxes, setting a minimum opening bid of $29,000.The planned sale creates major problems for the homeowner because of exactly where the 40-foot strip sits. Since the marked boundary runs within inches of his home's foundation, a sale to an outside buyer at auction could seriously limit access to his house, driveway, and utilities. Under local zoning and land use rules, selling the strip to an outside bidder could create a legal conflict over access rights, possibly leaving the homeowner without clear rights to reach parts of his own home. Reporting by AOL News noted that the homeowner has tried to negotiate directly with Oklahoma County commissioners and county assessors to fix the administrative error or remove the land from the upcoming auction before bidding starts.The land dispute was placed on the official agenda during Oklahoma County commission meetings, where officials discussed the legal status of county-acquired property and tax sale procedures. According to meeting minutes available on DocketCity, county boards must follow state legal rules when it comes to selling tax-delinquent properties. Once a property is formally certified for tax sale, removing it from the process often requires court involvement or clear approval from the board to pause the auction. Oklahoma County officials said tax sales are carried out strictly under state property laws to resolve long-standing ownership gaps and return unclaimed land to active tax rolls. The homeowner continues to seek a resolution with county officials or legal counsel to secure ownership of the 40-foot strip and stop the land from going up for auction.
Article Summary: Homeowner bought five acres of land from his grandfather in 1994, believing the sale covered the full area around his family home. For 32 years, he mowed the yard, paid property taxes, and lived on the land without ever hearing about any boundary dispute from local government. The issue came up recently when Oklahoma County officials reviewed regional land records and found an unassigned, tax- delinquent strip measuring 40 feet wide right along his house. The county listed the narrow strip of land for public auction to recover unpaid taxes, setting a minimum opening bid of $29,000.

Article Title: Kentucky man won $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in 2025; now arrested for fifth time after being found intoxicated in Walmart car park
Article Text:
Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running Mustang

How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prize

Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot win

February arrest involved an intimidation charge

Burglary and marijuana charges followed in March

July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegations

Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal cases

James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.The latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.Farthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Farthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.In February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Farthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.In late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.The September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.As of September 23, 2026, the public intoxication case remained pending in Scott County District Court, with no confirmed outcome of the scheduled arraignment.The jackpot that promised a new beginning has instead been followed by a string of legal troubles. Fortune's wheel turns without warning, and wealth offers no guarantee of a steady life.
Article Summary: James Farthing won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025. He has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol- related impairment.

Article Title: In 2015, a Minnesota couple entered the Boundary Waters to oppose a proposed mine; 366 days and 2,000 miles later, they emerged without crossing a road or entering a building
Article Text:
Image of Dave and Amy Freeman standing together alongside Pose Lake in Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. Credits - Instagram/freemanexplore, Wikipedia

A wilderness with robust federal safeguards

Image showing Dave and Amy Freeman holding hands together alongside The BWCAW within the Superior National Forest. Credits – Instagram/freemanexplore, Wikipedia

An extension of years spent teaching via travel

On rare occasions, activists decide to use their presence as a point of contention, remaining in the area they wish to be protected for so long that it is impossible to ignore. This was the motivation behind one of the more unusual protest trips of the past ten years, which was conducted solely by foot, kayak, and ski into Minnesota's far north.Ely, Minnesota, wilderness guides Dave and Amy Freeman entered the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness on September 23, 2015, and didn’t leave until September 23, 2016, living for 366 continuous days in the wild, without crossing a road or going into a building. Their expedition carried them over 2,000 miles by canoe, foot, ski, snowshoe and dog team over some 500 lakes, rivers and streams, camping at some 120 different places through all four seasons. The pair travelled there in support of the Save the Boundary Waters group, which has fought for years against proposed sulphide ore copper mining near the border of the wilderness, due to fears that mine runoff might damage the watershed's interconnected lakes for generations.The Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness is a million-plus acres of wilderness in the northern portion of Superior National Forest and extends almost 150 miles along the international boundary with Canada.The US Forest Service manages the land and classified the area as protected wilderness under the Wilderness Act of 1964. Development and motorized activity are therefore restricted within its borders, though traditional non-motorized aids like sailboats, sleds and dog teams remain permitted. That legal protection applies to the wilderness itself, but the watershed that feeds its lakes stretches beyond the boundary line into places where mineral leases have been proposed, which is precisely the gap the Freemans wanted to point out.It wasn’t just camping to live in the outdoors for a full year. The duo fell through ice, were stalked at a distance by wolves, drank directly from the lakes and used a small sailboat and sled to transport supplies between seasons. Even so, they used satellite technology to stay in touch with schools and supporters throughout the year, turning what could have been a private ordeal into a public campaign followed by hundreds of thousands of people online. On the last day, when they eventually paddled out, dozens of canoes and a crowd of well-wishers gathered at Ely to welcome them home.The wilderness year was not a one-off adventure but part of a longer pattern in the Freemans’ lives. The couple had already kayaked, canoed, dog-sledded and hiked across North America on a three-year, more than 11,000-mile trek and separately paddled 2,000 miles over 100 days from Minnesota to Washington to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Wilderness Act. Each of these expeditions was linked to their nonprofit, Wilderness Classroom , which uses the trips to teach literacy, critical thinking and environmental awareness to tens of thousands of school children who follow along remotely, instead of in person.The mix of endurance travel and education brought the pair accolades beyond the campaign itself, including inclusion on National Geographic’s Adventurers of the Year list and a written account of their wilderness year that won a regional book prize. The campaign they supported continued to gain political momentum in the years that followed, with government reviews and leasing decisions around the planned mining sites changing back and forth depending on the administration in office at any given time.They did not write letters or deliver speeches from afar but lived in the landscape they wanted to protect through blizzards, thaws and every season in between, believing that a prolonged presence would be more effective than words. That effort continues to shape the discussion around one of America's most visited wilderness areas, a watershed where the mining fight is still unresolved: federal protections were rolled back by Congress in 2026, even as Minnesota's state government has moved to block new mining leases nearby.
Article Summary: Dave and Amy Freeman spent a year living in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in Minnesota's far north. They travelled by canoe, foot, ski, snowshoe and dog team over some 500 lakes, rivers and streams, camping at some 120 different places through all four seasons. The pair travelled there in support of the Save the Boundaries group, which has fought for years against proposed sulphide ore copper mining near the border of the wilderness.

Article Title: A $12,055 library bill was waived after a New Hampshire man returned an 1894 magazine that had been overdue for 48,220 days, or 132 years
Article Text:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine / Concord Public Library | Wikimedia Commons

The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine

The magazine had been sitting in his home

The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine

The fine was theoretical, not a bill he had to pay

Under the policy, existing fines were frozen and patrons would no longer accumulate overdue charges for ordinary late returns | Wikimedia Commons

What happens to the 1894 issue now

John Hanson walked into the Concord Public Library in New Hampshire with a September 1894 issue of. The 84-year-old Barrington resident had kept the magazine for decades, and when he returned it in September 2026, the item was 48,220 days overdue. That would have amounted to a $12,055 penalty under the library’s previous fine system, but he did not have to pay it because the library had begun a year-long freeze on overdue fines.Hanson told library staff that he did not know exactly how the magazine ended up in his possession; it had been in his home for years before he decided to return it after learning about Concord Public Library’s new fine-free policy. The item was a September 1894 issue of, which was a publication that was already more than a century old when Hanson brought it back. FOX 5 reported that the magazine had been 48,220 days overdue according to the library’s calculation. Concord Public Library had announced that beginning September 1, 2026, it would freeze fines for 12 months while the city evaluated the effects of moving toward a fine-free system. Under the policy, existing fines were frozen and patrons would no longer accumulate overdue charges for ordinary late returns. Hanson’s return therefore came during a period when the library was actively encouraging people to bring back overdue materials without getting worried about accumulated penalties.The $12,055 figure represents what the late fee would have been under the calculation reported by the library, and Hanson did not actually receive a $12,055 bill when he returned the magazine. FOX 5 reported that the library had expected overdue materials to come back during the fine freeze but did not expect something from the late 19th century to turn up. The magazine was not returned to normal circulation because of its age, and library staff said that it could instead be preserved in the Concord Room.Concord said that its year-long experiment would allow officials to evaluate what happens when overdue fines are removed as a barrier to returning materials. The freeze covers current fines for 12 months, although the library retains restrictions for lost or damaged items and certain overdue accounts.The case also shows us how a policy that is designed to encourage ordinary overdue returns can produce unexpected results when an item has been missing for generations. Staff could now treat its return as an opportunity to preserve an unusual piece of the library’s collection history instead of treating the magazine simply as a long-overdue loan.UPI reported that library officials said it would not be returned to circulation and could instead be displayed in the building’s Concord Room, which gives the returned issue a different status from an ordinary overdue item. It has become an archival object that is connected to the library’s own history, complete with evidence of its original circulation.The episode also illustrates why the library’s fine-free experiment matters in practical terms, since Hanson said that he decided to return the magazine after hearing about the freeze, and the library received an item that had been missing since the 19th century. For Concord Public Library, the September 1894 issue came back in its possession, 48,220 days after its due date, and the $12,055 theoretical fine did not have to be paid.
Article Summary: John Hanson, 84, returned a September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine to the Concord Public Library in New Hampshire. The magazine was 48,220 days overdue, which would have amounted to a $12,055 penalty under the library’s previous fine system. Hanson did not have to pay the fine because the library had begun a year-long freeze on overdue fines.

Article Title: 'Restore access': US court temporarily blocks Trump's ban on TV networks from White House
Article Text: A US court on Thursday directed the Trump administration to reverse its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from reporting inside the White House grounds.Blocking the ban temporarily, US district Judge Tim Kelly said that the decision was likely unconstitutional.“The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest,” the judge said.This comes after US President Donald Trump announced the ban on the three outlets in a social media post on Friday, writing that he was banning the media outlets for reporting "fake news."Trump announced the move in a post on Truth Social, saying the ban was effective immediately. “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW (who recently changed their name from MSNBC due to lack of viewership and credibility!), and Politico (The recipients of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription, an All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them ‘alive. ’ Seems like corruption to me!), from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” he said.Trump also said he would announce additional media outlets that could face similar restrictions. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.Later, the three outlets filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, saying that they were pursuing legal action to “defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports”.
