Article Summary: US President Donald Trump announced the ban on the three outlets in a social media post on Friday, writing that he was banning the media outlets for reporting "fake news" The three outlets filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, saying that they were pursuing legal action to “defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports”

Article Title: Nebraska couple to auction 350-vehicle classic Chevrolet collection after housing development near property; hundreds of Impalas, Caprices and other vehicles from the 1950s to 1970s included
Article Text:
Image: KMTV

Nebraska couple's 350-vehicle Chevrolet collection faces auction

Image : KMTV

Hundreds of Impalas among the classic Chevrolets

Collection includes Chevrolet pickups and other vehicles

Housing development changed the situation

Couple plans to retain a smaller collection

Auction scheduled for October 3

Most vehicles are projects or restoration candidates

Four decades of collecting come to a turning point

A Nebraska couple is preparing to auction about 350 classic Chevrolet vehicles after development around their property led to code-enforcement pressure over their decades-old collection. Tim and Mary Robinson of Saunders County have spent more than 40 years collecting full-size Chevrolets, building a collection that eventually grew to nearly 450 vehicles. The cars being offered include hundreds of Impalas, along with Bel Airs, Caprices, Biscaynes, Nomads, station wagons, convertibles, Corvettes and Chevrolet pickups. VanDerBrink Auctions will conduct the live and online sale on October 3, 2026, in Fremont. The Robinsons plan to retain a smaller personal collection while hoping the vehicles find new owners who appreciate their history.Tim Robinson's interest in classic Chevrolet vehicles developed over several decades. According to VanDerBrink Auctions, Robinson worked at Road Runner Auto Salvage, where he became familiar with full-size Chevrolets and developed a passion for the vehicles. He and his family later travelled around the US searching for Chevrolet models, particularly vehicles from the 1955 to 1970 period.Over more than 40 years, the collection expanded to almost 450 Chevrolet classics. The National Impala Association separately reported that Robinson had accumulated more than 400 vehicles over four decades. The organisation also reported meeting Robinson and his family at its 2025 convention.Chevrolet Impalas make up a significant portion of the collection. VanDerBrink Auctions says about 75% of the collection consists of Impalas dating from 1958 to 1970. The collection also contains Bel Airs, Caprices, Biscaynes, Nomads, station wagons, convertibles and other full-size Chevrolet models. The auction catalogue includes vehicles from several decades, including 1950s and 1960s Chevrolet models. Some are complete vehicles, while others are project cars or vehicles intended for restoration or use as parts.The collection is not limited to passenger cars. VanDerBrink estimates that about 50 Chevrolet pickups are included, along with other trucks and Chevrolet vehicles. The auction catalogue includes examples such as a 1962 Chevrolet C10 pickup and a 1969 Chevrolet 92 van. A small number of vehicles from other General Motors brands are also included in the sale. The auction listing mentions Pontiac and Oldsmobile vehicles alongside the large Chevrolet collection.The decision to sell much of the collection followed development around the Robinsons' property. KMTV reported that the couple received a notice in January 2026 after a housing developer purchased land surrounding their collection. According to the report, they were given only days to decide whether to fight to keep the collection or sell it. The National Impala Association also reported that complaints and subsequent local enforcement action were involved in the dispute. It said the situation ultimately resulted in Robinson having to substantially reduce his collection. The available reporting therefore establishes a sequence involving the surrounding land purchase, development, complaints and code-enforcement pressure, followed by the Robinsons' decision to sell a large portion of their collection. It is more precise to describe the situation this way than to state that the developer directly ordered the couple to sell the vehicles.The auction will not mark the complete end of the Robinsons' involvement with classic vehicles. The couple plans to retain a smaller personal collection, according to local reporting. They have also expressed hope that the vehicles being sold will go to buyers who appreciate their history. The cars have personal significance for the family after decades of collecting. The sale therefore represents a major reduction in a collection that had become a substantial part of the Robinsons' lives.VanDerBrink Auctions is scheduled to conduct the Robinson Chevrolet Collection auction on October 3, 2026, beginning at 9am Central in Fremont, Nebraska. The sale will offer both onsite and online bidding. A preview is scheduled for October 2 from 10am to 5pm.The auctioneer describes the sale as approximately 350 classic Chevrolet vehicles, while its description of the Robinson collection says it had grown to almost 450 vehicles. The current Proxibid catalogue lists 349 lots.The collection's size does not mean all of the cars are fully restored classics. VanDerBrink describes many of the vehicles as restoration projects, project cars or parts vehicles. This means prospective buyers will find vehicles in different conditions rather than hundreds of ready-to-display show cars.The range of vehicles is nevertheless notable, particularly because of the concentration of full-size Chevrolet models from the 1950s through the 1970s. The collection includes numerous Impalas alongside Caprices, Bel Airs, Biscaynes, Nomads, wagons, pickups and other Chevrolet vehicles.After more than 40 years of collecting, the Robinsons are now preparing to disperse most of their Chevrolet collection through the October auction. The sale follows development around their property and the enforcement issues reported by the family and local media.While hundreds of vehicles will leave the property, the Robinsons plan to keep a smaller collection. The October 3 auction will give collectors an opportunity to acquire vehicles from a collection that accumulated hundreds of Chevrolet models across several decades.
Article Summary: Tim and Mary Robinson of Saunders County have spent more than 40 years collecting full-size Chevrolets. Their collection eventually grew to nearly 450 vehicles, including hundreds of Impalas, Bel Airs, Caprices, Biscaynes, Nomads, station wagons, convertibles, Corvettes and Chevrolet pickups. VanDerBrink Auctions will conduct the live and online sale on October 3, 2026, in Fremont, Nebraska.

Article Title: In 2007, a rare Atari game surfaced at a garage sale; 19 years later, it sold with its original cassette for $6,562.50
Article Text:
Representative Image of the Atari 2600 game Red Sea Crossing with its cartridge, coloring book, and audiocassette, showcasing Christian themes (AI Generated)

The Atari game placed players in the story of Moses

Its only known advertisement appeared in Christianity Today

A garage-sale discovery brought the game back into view

The cassette made the 2026 auction unusual

Red Sea Crossing sold for $6,562.50

A rare Christian-themed Atari 2600 game that surfaced at a garage sale in 2007 has sold at auction for $6,562.50. Red Sea Crossing, released through mail order in 1983, was offered by Heritage Auctions with an accompanying audiocassette. The sale marked the first time the cassette itself had been presented at auction, according to the auction house. Steve Schustack created the game and takes its inspiration from the biblical story of Moses parting the Red Sea. Players guide Moses between walls of water while avoiding obstacles and the pursuing Egyptian army. The cartridge was sold at Heritage Auctions’ June 12–13, 2026 Video Games Signature Auction, where it was listed as lot 28003.Red Sea Crossing was released for the Atari 2600 in 1983 by Inspirational Video Concepts. Unlike many commercial console games of the period, it was not distributed through ordinary retail channels. Heritage describes it as a mail-order release with a Christian theme. The gameplay centres on Moses crossing the Red Sea. The player must guide him between the parted waters while avoiding hazards including seaweed, giant clams and the Egyptian army.The game also includes a fish that acts as a time limit, requiring players to reach the end of the screen before it catches up with Moses. The package was unusual in another respect. Instead of being accompanied only by a conventional instruction manual, the game was originally sold with a colouring book and an explanatory audiocassette connected to the story of the Exodus. Heritage identifies the cassette as being narrated by Dale Evans Rogers.The game’s limited distribution has contributed to its rarity. Heritage states that its only marketing was an advertisement in the October 7, 1983 issue of Christianity Today. The advertisement offered the game by mail order and helped establish that the obscure cartridge had genuinely been released. The game’s existence was not widely documented for many years. A copy discovered at a Cincinnati rummage sale in 2007 became the subject of discussion among Atari collectors, who worked to identify its developer and establish whether it was an authentic commercial release. A surviving advertisement found in Christianity Today in 2011 provided important evidence that the game had been marketed in 1983. Heritage describes the title as one of the rarest commercially released console games ever produced. However, estimates of how many cartridges were made vary among historical accounts, so the precise size of the original production run remains difficult to establish.The 2007 discovery was significant because Red Sea Crossing had largely disappeared from public knowledge. The game was not part of Atari’s mainstream catalogue, and its mail-order distribution meant that comparatively few examples were documented by collectors. After the cartridge was found, members of the Atari community investigated its origins and connected it to Steve Schustack. Historical accounts identify Schustack as the programmer and describe the game as an independent project released through Inspirational Video Concepts. The discovery eventually led to renewed interest in the game and to the appearance of additional examples. One copy sold at auction in 2012 for $10,400, while another copy that surfaced in Philadelphia was also sold that year. The earlier sales helped establish Red Sea Crossing as a sought-after rarity among Atari collectors.The Heritage lot consisted of the Atari 2600 cartridge and an accompanying cassette. The auction house described the cassette as particularly notable because it was the first time the tape itself had been presented at auction. That distinction matters because the cassette was part of the game’s original package but has been much less frequently documented than the cartridge. The game’s historical descriptions consistently mention the colouring book and audio recording, but surviving examples of the complete package are considerably harder to trace than reproductions and loose cartridges. Heritage described both items in the lot as being in excellent condition. The cartridge and cassette were nevertheless sold untested and as-is, with no returns.Heritage Auctions listed the item as lot 28003 in its 2026 Video Games Signature Auction. The auction took place on June 12 and 13, with the Red Sea Crossing lot recorded as sold on June 12 for $6,562.50. Heritage’s listing records 36 bids and registered phone bidders, with a 25% buyer’s premium applying to the lot. The result adds a new chapter to the history of a game that was originally sold through a single religious-magazine advertisement, rediscovered at a garage sale and later recognised as one of the most elusive Atari 2600 releases. The 2026 sale was especially notable not simply because of the cartridge’s rarity, but because it brought an original accompanying cassette into the auction record for the first time.
Article Summary: Red Sea Crossing was released for the Atari 2600 in 1983 by Inspirational Video Concepts. Unlike many commercial console games of the period, it was not distributed through ordinary retail channels. Its only marketing was an advertisement in the October 7, 1983 issue of Christianity Today. The game’s existence was not widely documented for many years. A copy discovered at a Cincinnati rummage sale in 2007 became the subject of discussion among Atari collectors.

Article Title: An Arkansas mom secretly cleared $67,676.60 in family debt in 45 days while her husband had no idea; social media followers helped erase their mortgage, truck loan and bakery business debt
Article Text:
31-year-old mother revealed how an ambitious personal challenge turned into a social media movement involving thousands of strangers.

A debt-free goal that started quietly

Turning social media into micropayments

Strangers become the mountain movers

$67,676.60 cleared in 45 days

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Erika's journey inspired you the most? Her determination Innovative use of social media Creating community support Managing family responsibilities 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

For 45 days, Erika Dison carried a secret that could change her family's financial future. While her husband, Cody, continued their everyday life in central Arkansas, she was quietly working to erase every dollar of their $67,676.60 debt. By the time she finally revealed what she had been doing, the couple's mortgage, truck loan and bakery business debt had been cleared.In an exclusive report by PEOPLE, the 31-year-old mother revealed how an ambitious personal challenge turned into a social media movement involving thousands of strangers.Dison had originally planned to become debt-free by December 31, 2027. The family's outstanding balances included the remainder of their mortgage, Cody's truck loan and a business loan Dison had taken to expand her home-based sourdough bakery, Rosie.As the PEOPLE report stated, the family carried no student loans or revolving credit card debt, and Dison's car was already paid off. Still, seeing the remaining total in one place clarified the scale of the challenge. Her motivation was tied to a larger family dream. She wanted to raise the couple's three children, ages 7, 3 and 7 months, on a small farm where they could grow up around animals and learn about food and farming.Rather than telling Cody about her accelerated plan, Dison created secret TikTok and Facebook accounts and began documenting her progress.Dison, who has an accounting background and a strong interest in numbers, created a system that linked her social media activity directly to debt payments. Every follower, like, comment, share and save on her videos represented a dollar amount she would put toward the family's balances. She tracked the numbers in a small red notebook, recording the payments, remaining debt and percentage completed each day.Initially, the challenge was entirely self-funded. Money generated by Rosie's weekly preorders, farmers markets, events, the Little Pink Bread Shed and stores carrying her products went toward the debt.About a week into the challenge, followers began asking how they could support the effort. Dison responded by opening a Shopify store selling sourdough starter, recipes and merchandise, while supporters could also contribute through GoFundMe, Cash App, PayPal and Venmo.As her videos attracted more attention, the online community surrounding the challenge adopted the name Mountain Movers, inspired by a biblical passage that had encouraged Dison to take on the financial challenge. The movement also expanded beyond debt repayment. Through a program called Bake It Forward, followers could sponsor bread, cookies and brownies that Dison would distribute locally to people experiencing food insecurity. The purchases generated bakery income while allowing the online community to support a local cause. And behind the scenes, however, Cody remained unaware.Dison continued to manage the challenge while maintaining the family's normal routines. She reduced spending in subtle ways, planned meals around food already in the refrigerator, freezer and pantry, and kept the children from discovering the secret.The pressure intensified as the challenge continued, particularly on Day 35, which was Cody's birthday. By then, Dison was juggling homeschooling, caring for three young children, running the household and increasing her bakery workload. On Day 45, she finally reached the $67,676.60 target. Around $40,000 came through GoFundMe, Cash App, PayPal and Venmo. Another roughly $10,000 came from Rosie, recipe sales and Mountain Mover merchandise, with the remainder coming from the family's checking account and bakery income. Dison did not receive an inheritance or unexpected windfall and did not earn money directly from TikTok. She then sat down with Cody after the children went to bed and handed him a letter explaining the entire challenge.The reveal video later reached a much wider audience after it was accidentally posted to her main TikTok account. It surpassed 1 million views within 24 hours and approached 12 million views over five days.With the debt gone, Dison's focus has shifted toward the family's next chapter: potentially building a forever home, expanding their farm dreams and helping other families find their own way through financial challenges. The Mountain Movers community that grew around her secret is now turning its attention toward helping others tackle their own financial goals, the exclusive report concludes.Image Courtesy: istock and People
Article Summary: Erika Dison, 31, of central Arkansas, had originally planned to become debt-free by December 31, 2027. The family's outstanding balances included the remainder of their mortgage, Cody's truck loan and a business loan Dison had taken to expand her home-based sourdough bakery, Rosie. She created secret TikTok and Facebook accounts and began documenting her progress.

Article Title: Kabul-Islamabad tensions soar: Pakistan strikes 10 sites in Afghanistan after drone attacks
Article Text:
Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid had denied on Wednesday that Afghan Taliban forces carried out attacks against Pakistan.

Pakistan accuses Taliban of backing militants

Escalation threatens mediation efforts

Pakistan said early Thursday that it had carried out airstrikes on 10 sites in Afghanistan that it said were used to launch drone attacks against Pakistan.Pakistan's information minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes targeted sites linked to what Pakistan described as attempted attacks from Afghan territory. He said the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate” and limited to military objectives.The announcement came after Pakistani officials said Afghan Taliban forces had launched eight rudimentary drones and shelled Pakistani border posts after Pakistani troops foiled what they described as an attempted cross-border infiltration by militants.There was no immediate response from Kabul to the latest Pakistani strikes. Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid had denied on Wednesday that Afghan Taliban forces carried out attacks against Pakistan.According to four Pakistani officials, the attempted infiltration took place near Afghan border posts in Paktia and Nangarhar provinces. The militants were described by Islamabad as Fitna-ul-Khawarij, a term it uses for the Pakistani Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).The officials said Afghan Taliban forces allegedly provided support to the militants and later fired mortars and other heavy weapons at Pakistani border posts after the infiltration attempt was thwarted. Pakistani forces responded with artillery fire targeting Taliban border posts, mortar positions and defensive sites.The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the latest escalation publicly, said some Afghan Taliban positions were subsequently abandoned and that there were casualties. The accounts could not be independently verified.Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Taliban government of allowing militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegations.Pakistani officials also said eight drones launched from Afghanistan were shot down before they could reach Kohat and the border town of Torkham. They said the drones caused no damage.The latest confrontation follows Pakistani airstrikes on eastern Afghanistan on Monday, which Islamabad said targeted militant hideouts. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, while Afghan authorities reported at least three civilian deaths and four injuries. The UN mission in Afghanistan confirmed the civilian casualties, and Kabul formally protested the strikes.The latest fighting threatens mediation efforts by China, Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which have been seeking to ease tensions between Islamabad and Kabul.The escalation also follows a series of deadly militant attacks in Pakistan's north-west. Six Pakistani security personnel were killed in a shootout with militants in Hangu, while a suicide bombing and subsequent gunbattle at a police compound in nearby Kohat killed at least 21 people.
Article Summary: Pakistani officials say Afghan Taliban forces launched eight rudimentary drones and shelled Pakistani border posts. Pakistani troops foiled what they described as an attempted cross-border infiltration by militants. Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid had denied on Wednesday that Afghan Taliban. forces carried out attacks against Pakistan.

Article Title: Pakistan wants to be the Muslim world's security guard. Can its economy pay the bill?
Article Text:
Can Pakistan afford to be the Muslim world's 'security guard'?

Trilateral defence pact

From bilateral ties to a three-way defence pact

The first real test came quickly

Nato-style defence pact: Who bring what?

Pakistan is trying to become an arms seller, too

The China factor

Development is the opportunity cost

Saudi Arabia is both security partner and financial lifeline

Islamabad is still dependent on external financing

The military's growing regional role

A bigger military does not automatically mean a stronger state

The real test is economic endurance

Pakistan wants a bigger military role. Can its economy keep up?

The promise and the hard reality

Pakistan is betting that military muscle can buy it a bigger seat at the global table. Islamabad has deepened defence ties with Saudi Arabia and Turkey through the Mecca pact, sought a larger role in Gulf security, marketed its fighter jets and drones abroad and cast itself as an emerging security partner across the Muslim world.But the bigger Pakistan’s ambitions become, thebigger the question: How much can its military and economy actually carry?The country is trying to project strategic strength while simultaneously operating under a $7 billon International Monetary Fund programme, managing large external financing needs and trying to keep its foreign exchange reserves above critical levels. Its latest federal budget increased defence spending sharply while cutting the federal development allocation.That tension is becoming harder to ignore.In June, Pakistan unveiled an PKR 18.77 trillion budget for the financial year beginning July 2026. Defence spending was raised 18% to PKR 3 trillion, while federal development spending was cut to PKR 1 trillion. The Shehbaz Sharif-led government is also targeting PKR 15.26 trillion in tax revenue and an overall fiscal deficit of PKR 5.23 trillion, or 3.6% of GDP.Pakistan finance minister Muhammad Aurangzeb justified the defence increase by pointing to regional uncertainty, saying defence spending had been raised “to make the country invincible”.However, the desperation to attain “invincibility” must be attributed to the setback Islamabad suffered at India’s hands during Operation Sindoor, when Pakistan lost multiple crucial airbases and key military infrastructure.The numbers underline the dilemma facing Islamabad: Pakistan wants to be a security provider abroad at a time when its government is still trying to create enough fiscal space to stabilise the economy at home.The biggest symbol of Pakistan's expanding security role is its new defence arrangement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey.The three Islamic nations in August formed a Nato-style Mecca Pact. The agreement becomes crucial as the pact, also included a nuclear power.On August 7, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries is to be treated as an attack on all. The agreement was signed in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.Erdogan described the pact as being based on “collective deterrence”, while saying it was not directed against any particular country. Sharif called it a “historic pact” and described it as a “shield of peace”.Pakistan's foreign minister Ishaq Dar has stressed that the agreement is “purely defensive in nature” and open to other countries that accept its principles.The arrangement brings together three countries with very different strengths.Pakistan has a large, combat-experienced military and is the only nuclear-armed country in the Muslim world. Saudi Arabia has enormous financial resources and significant influence across the Arab world. Turkey has Nato's second-largest army and a rapidly expanding defence industry.On paper, the combination is formidable.In practice, however, the pact immediately raises questions about what Pakistan can actually contribute if Saudi Arabia faces a major security crisis.Those questions have become more pressing as Saudi Arabia has come under attack from Yemen's Houthis.The defence agreement was signed against the backdrop of a rapidly changing Middle East. Since then, Iran-backed Houthi attacks have intensified, targeting Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping routes.The issue has already forced Islamabad to clarify how far its treaty obligations extend.In September, Pakistan took a U-turn, saying there had been no discussion of a military response under the defence pact following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Islamabad remained committed to the agreement but added that action would come “when the time comes”.That careful wording illustrates the challenge.A collective-defence agreement can enhance deterrence without automatically requiring a country to enter every conflict involving its partner. But the credibility of such an arrangement ultimately depends on what happens when the security commitment is tested.Turkey has already signalled a willingness to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia under the pact.Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan said Riyadh could have military needs, particularly technical ones, and that Ankara would have no problem meeting them.Pakistan, meanwhile, has pledged support for Saudi Arabia but has so far avoided spelling out the precise circumstances under which it would deploy combat forces.That caution is understandable. Pakistan has its own security challenges, a difficult economic position and a military stretched across multiple fronts.There is another side to Islamabad's new defence diplomacy.Pakistan does not want to remain only a buyer of military hardware or a provider of troops and security expertise. It increasingly wants to become a defence exporter.That effort received a major boost after the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, when Pakistani officials began marketing the country’s military equipment as “combat tested”.However, the reality was totally different. Pakistan indulged in self-congratulation and boasted about its military performance despite losing a sizable chunk of its military infrastructure, including targets in Rawalpindi, the country’s military capital, located barely 15 kilometres from the political capital, Islamabad.Pakistan’s two highest authorities, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and field marshal Asim Munir , also repeatedly credited US President Donald Trump for brokering the ceasefire, going as far as backing a Nobel Peace Prize for him.The reality, however, was that Pakistan’s Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) had approached his Indian counterpart and pleaded for an end to India’s counterterror operation.That apparent attempt to impress the MAGA supremo earned both men Trump’s attention. Munir was described by Trump as his “favourite field marshal”, while Sharif was praised as a “fantastic” prime minister.Reuters reported in January that Pakistan was in discussions with 13 countries over possible defence sales, with six to eight negotiations described as being at an advanced stage. The discussions involved JF-17 fighter jets, training aircraft, drones, air defence systems and armoured vehicles.Potential customers mentioned in the report included Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, Sudan, Nigeria, Morocco and Ethiopia, while Pakistan has also acknowledged discussions involving Bangladesh and Iraq.The pitch is straightforward: Relatively capable equipment at a lower price.Reuters reported that Pakistani JF-17s are being offered at roughly $30 million to $40 million, significantly below some Western alternatives.Pakistan's defence production minister Raza Hayat Harraj told Reuters that there were “a lot of queries” and that Islamabad was negotiating, while stressing that details of individual negotiations remained confidential.If even a portion of those talks turn into contracts, they could provide Pakistan with something it badly needs: foreign exchange earnings and a larger domestic defence-production ecosystem.The country's private defence sector is already being pulled into the effort.Reuters reported that Pakistani companies are producing reconnaissance and kamikaze drones, with military demand helping drive the expansion of private-sector defence manufacturing.That could eventually create a cycle in which military investment generates exports, exports generate foreign currency and foreign currency helps finance further industrial development.But that cycle is not guaranteed.Pakistan's defence-export ambitions are also tied closely to China.The JF-17 is jointly developed by Pakistan and China, while much of Pakistan's broader military inventory has Chinese origins or components. That gives Islamabad access to a major defence-industrial partner, but it also means that Pakistan cannot always make export decisions in isolation.SIPRI researcher Siemon Wezeman told Reuters that it was unclear how many reported JF-17 discussions would ultimately become firm contracts. He also pointed to possible complications involving proposed sales to countries under UN arms embargoes.For Islamabad, therefore, becoming a defence exporter is not simply a matter of finding customers.It requires production capacity, financing, political relationships, technology partnerships and careful management of export controls.And there is another problem: Defence exports may take years to generate substantial returns, while the costs of maintaining a modern military are immediate.The domestic bill is much larger than the defence allocationPakistan's PKR 3 trillion defence allocation is only one part of the country's security burden.The economy must simultaneously finance debt servicing, public-sector salaries and pensions, energy subsidies and infrastructure, while meeting IMF conditions.The 2026-27 budget envisages a federal deficit of PKR 7.02 trillion. At the broader level, after factoring in a projected provincial surplus, the fiscal deficit target is PKR 5.23 trillion, equivalent to 3.6% of GDP.The government is also expected to generate PKR 15.26 trillion in tax revenue, despite the Federal Board of Revenue having missed its previous target.This is where Pakistan's defence ambitions collide with a familiar domestic problem: the state needs more revenue, but expanding the tax base is politically and economically difficult.Reuters noted that sectors such as agriculture, retail and real estate remain difficult to tax fully, increasing the pressure on salaried workers and businesses already within the tax system.At the same time, Islamabad has promised the IMF a primary surplus of 2% of GDP.In simple terms, the government needs to collect more than it spends before interest payments are taken into account.That leaves limited room for additional spending, whether on welfare, infrastructure or defence.The clearest illustration of that squeeze is the development budget.As defence spending rose to PKR 3 trillion, federal development spending was set at PKR 1 trillion.That does not mean every rupee spent on defence comes directly at the expense of a school, hospital or road. Pakistan's budget is considerably more complicated than that.But it does show the hierarchy of priorities in a country where fiscal resources are limited.Security has become a politically difficult area to cut, particularly after the 2025 conflict with India and amid continuing militant violence inside Pakistan.The Islamabad authorities also face two resentment-filled fronts in Balochistan and PoK, where growing discontent is being fuelled by economic hardship and demands for independence and autonomy.Development spending, meanwhile, can be delayed, reduced or shifted to provinces.The result is a structural trade-off: Pakistan wants to maintain military readiness against external threats while also addressing the economic conditions that underpin long-term national power.A country can buy aircraft, missiles and drones. It cannot build sustained strategic power without economic growth, industrial capacity, energy security and human capital.Pakistan's relationship with Saudi Arabia makes this tension even more interesting.Riyadh is not merely a defence partner. It has repeatedly played a role in Pakistan's financial stabilisation.In April, Saudi Arabia agreed to provide Pakistan with an additional $3 billion deposit to help it meet a $3.5 billion repayment to the UAE. The assistance came on top of the renewal of a $5 billion Saudi deposit arrangement.Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves stood at around $16.4 billion at the end of March, according to Reuters, while the country remained under its $7 billion IMF programme.The same relationship that gives Islamabad an important strategic role in Gulf security also provides financial support when its external accounts come under pressure.That creates mutual dependence.Saudi Arabia gains access to a nuclear-armed security partner with decades of military cooperation. Pakistan gains a wealthy strategic partner willing to provide financial backing.But financial assistance is not the same thing as a permanent solution to Pakistan's economic constraints.Pakistan's dependence on outside financing remains visible in its dealings with both China and the United States.Finance minister Aurangzeb said this month that Islamabad plans to seek an expansion of its 30 billion yuan currency-swap arrangement with China when it comes up for renewal in 2027. Reuters reported that the entire existing facility had been drawn.Pakistan is also seeking a $10 billion exchange stabilisation facility from Washington and expects a US decision within months, while talks are under way with US financing institutions over other projects.Aurangzeb called Islamabad's approach as an “and-and” strategy, arguing that relations with China and the US are not mutually exclusive.That balancing act mirrors Pakistan's broader foreign-policy strategy.It wants China for defence and infrastructure, Saudi Arabia for investment and financial support, Turkey for defence technology and strategic cooperation, and the US for access to Western financial institutions and markets.The difficulty is ensuring that these relationships produce economic capacity rather than simply postponing the next financing challenge.Pakistan's security role is nevertheless changing.The country has long maintained close military ties with Saudi Arabia. In September 2025, Islamabad and Riyadh signed a Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement stating that aggression against either country would be considered aggression against both.The military's growing role has almost made Rawalpindi a superior power centre in Pakistan compared to Islamabad. Pakistan has remained a country greatly influenced by its military. Asim Munir has been in power, seeking to supersede his predecessors, the military dictators.The de-facto head of Pakistan, Munir, has also gone far to advocate for peace, hosting talks for US-Iran peace.However, the peace talks failed.The newer three-way Mecca pact with Turkey expands that strategic architecture.Pakistan has also been trying to position itself as a mediator in the Middle East, including between Washington and Tehran, while simultaneously strengthening its security commitments to Riyadh.That is an unusually complicated diplomatic role.Islamabad must reassure Saudi Arabia without alienating Iran, maintain relations with the US without damaging its ties with China, and deepen military cooperation with Turkey while preserving its own strategic priorities.The danger is that a country with limited resources can accumulate commitments faster than it accumulates the capacity to fulfil them.Pakistan's military spending has been rising, but it remains much smaller in absolute terms than the defence budgets of its principal regional competitors.According to SIPRI, Pakistan's military expenditure rose 11% in 2025 to $11.9 billion. India's spending reached $92.1 billion, while Saudi Arabia spent $83.2 billion.The figures put Pakistan's strategy into perspective.It cannot realistically compete by matching the spending of larger economies. Its answer has instead been to seek cost-effective platforms, leverage Chinese technology, develop domestic production and use its military relationships as a source of strategic influence.That explains the emphasis on the JF-17, drones, training and military cooperation.Pakistan's defence industry can potentially occupy a niche between expensive Western systems and lower-cost equipment from other suppliers.The opportunity is real.But so is the capacity problem.A successful export industry needs factories that can produce at scale, supply chains that can withstand disruption, research and development, skilled workers and enough capital to keep investing.Pakistan's defence push is therefore not necessarily contradictory.A stronger defence industry could generate exports. Greater exports could bring in foreign currency. Joint production could create jobs and technology. Strategic partnerships could attract investment.But none of those outcomes are automatic.The immediate reality is that Islamabad is trying to maintain a large defence establishment while meeting IMF conditions, servicing debt and preserving foreign exchange reserves.The June budget already showed the pressure: Defence spending rose 18%, while federal development spending fell to PKR 1 trillion.Meanwhile, Pakistan's finance minister has warned that prolonged disruption in the Middle East could threaten the country's 4% growth target because of higher oil prices.That matters because Pakistan is heavily exposed to energy prices and external financing.A sustained geopolitical crisis could therefore produce the paradox Islamabad least wants: More demand for military readiness at precisely the moment when the economy has less room to pay for it.Pakistan is clearly trying to turn military capability into strategic influence.The new Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact gives Islamabad a larger role in Gulf security. Its relationship with Riyadh gives it both strategic and financial importance. Its defence industry is attracting foreign interest. Its JF-17 and drone programmes offer the prospect of export earnings. And its military's experience gives it diplomatic weight that exceeds the size of Pakistan's economy.But strategic influence has a price.Every new defence commitment creates an expectation of action. Every overseas weapons sale requires production capacity. Every new military platform creates long-term maintenance and training costs. And every promise made abroad ultimately has to be supported by an economy at home.That is Pakistan's central challenge.The country may be able to sell itself as a security provider, arms producer and strategic partner. But to sustain that image, it will need something more difficult than a new defence pact or a successful weapons demonstration: A durable economic base capable of paying for its ambitions.For now, Pakistan is attempting to build that base while simultaneously expanding its security commitments.The contradiction is visible in its own budget.Islamabad says it needs more defence spending because the region is becoming more dangerous. At the same time, it is cutting development spending because the government's finances are constrained.That may be manageable for a year or two.The bigger question is whether it can remain manageable for long enough for Pakistan's new defence promises to translate into lasting strategic power.
Article Summary: Pakistan is betting that military muscle can buy it a bigger seat at the global table. Islamabad has deepened defence ties with Saudi Arabia and Turkey through the Mecca pact. The bigger Pakistan’s ambitions become, thebigger the question: How much can its military and economy actually carry?

Article Title: Pakistan’s hidden health crisis: Children contract HIV after routine hospital care
Article Text:
Pakistan families allege children contracted HIV in hospitals (AP photo)

A routine visit to a hospital has turned into a life-changing ordeal for dozens of families in Pakistan, with parents alleging that their children contracted HIV while receiving medical care.The children were reportedly being treated for ordinary illnesses or undergoing routine procedures when, weeks or months later, they were found to be HIV positive, according to NPR. Their families say they had no other known explanation for how the children could have contracted the virus.Parents interviewed by NPR have pointed to poor infection-control practices at healthcare facilities, particularly the alleged reuse of syringes and needles during injections and intravenous (IV) treatment. They believe such practices may have exposed their children to HIV.The reported cases have brought devastating consequences for affected families. At least six children have died, while others face a lifetime of treatment and medical monitoring after being diagnosed with the virus.HIV weakens the immune system and currently has no cure, but antiretroviral treatment can control the virus and help people live longer, healthier lives.For families in the affected communities, however, the diagnosis has brought additional financial and social pressures, including the cost of medicines and repeated hospital visits and fears of stigma.Many parents are now seeking answers from the healthcare system. They want authorities to investigate how children with no apparent risk factors came to be infected and whether lapses in basic medical safety standards played a role.The allegations have also put a spotlight on infection-control practices at some Pakistani healthcare facilities. Families and rights advocates are calling for investigations, greater monitoring of hospitals and stricter safeguards around the use of medical equipment.
Article Summary: At least six children have died, while others face a lifetime of treatment and medical monitoring after being diagnosed with the virus. Parents point to poor infection-control practices at healthcare facilities, particularly the alleged reuse of syringes and needles during injections and intravenous treatment.

Article Title: Highways blocked, paramilitary deployed, hospitals on alert: Islamabad turns into fortress ahead of PTI march
Article Text:
The PTI march is scheduled for September 27

PTI refuses to back down

Pakistan on Wednesday blocked major highways leading to the capital, Islamabad, and deployed tens of thousands of security personnel ahead of a march planned by the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) seeking the release of its founder and jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan "Nearly 35,000 additional police and paramilitary personnel have been stationed in and around Islamabad," Reuters quoted an interior ministry official as saying."More have been deployed in other parts of Pakistan where Khan's supporters may gather," he added.Two major highways linking Islamabad to the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, governed by PTI, have also been closed until further notice, the National Highways Authority said.Shipping containers have been placed in recent days to barricade Islamabad's government district, home to parliament, the prime minister's residence and foreign embassies.Authorities have already put hospitals in Islamabad, including the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and Federal Government Polyclinic Hospital, on high alert until September 30.Police have also detained three of Khan's sisters and hundreds of party activists in recent days, citing the need to maintain public order.On Monday, Pakistan's interior minister, Mohsin Naqvi, warned that police had been told to respond "forcefully" if the march turned violent, adding, "It is not like they come and fire shots and you do nothing."The march is scheduled for September 27.However, PTI chairman Gohar Khan declared that the march would proceed despite the blockade.Khan, 73, was ousted as prime minister by parliament in a 2022 no-confidence vote. Cases against the cricketer-turned-politician, whose arrest in 2023 sparked nationwide riots, ranged from allegations involving state gifts and inciting violent attacks on military and state installations to an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one of his convictions have since been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.The PTI's planned march comes more than a month after the government defied a court order and refused to allow Khan to receive treatment at a private hospital, despite mounting concerns over his health.The protest also comes amid public discontent over inflation and rising fuel prices that has spread beyond Khan's core supporters.The PTI's previous large-scale protest, two years ago, ended in deadly clashes with security forces.
Article Summary: Pakistan deploys tens of thousands of security personnel ahead of a march. The march is planned by the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) It seeks the release of its founder and jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Khan was ousted as prime minister by parliament in a 2022 no-confidence vote.

Article Title: Gunmen kill 2 cops during polio vaccination drive in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
(Representative image): The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday.

Police officers killed during vaccination drive

Pakistan remains polio hotspot

Gunmen shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination workers in Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province on Tuesday. The officials said that the attack took place as health teams carried out a door-to-door campaign targeting more than 31 million children.The gunmen opened fire when Nushki district, polio workers were administering oral vaccine drops to children inside a home. The health workers escaped unharmed, local police official Munawar Zaman said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday.The latest campaign aims to vaccinate more than 31 million children across Pakistan against polio.Balochistan has faced repeated attacks by militant groups, including separatist militants. The Pakistani Taliban has also previously targeted security forces and civilians in Balochistan and other parts of the country.Pakistan's interior minister Mohsin Naqvi condemned the attack in a statement.Pakistan and neighbouring Afghanistan are the only countries where transmission of wild poliovirus has not been interrupted, according to the World Health Organisation.Security concerns have repeatedly complicated vaccination efforts in Pakistan, with polio workers and the police personnel assigned to protect them facing attacks during previous campaigns.
Article Summary: Gunmen shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination workers in Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province. The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

Article Title: 'Mass casualty' alert? Pakistan hospitals clear beds ahead of PTI protest
Article Text:
Protests in Pakistan (Representative image)

Imran Khan's family detained

Hospitals in Islamabad have allegedly been ordered to prepare for a possible “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident” ahead of a planned September 27 protest by jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The instructions to Islamabad hospitals called for all scheduled elective surgeries to be postponed indefinitely and surgical departments to be prepared for a possible surge in patients, according to documents reviewed by Drop Site.Medical and support staff were ordered to remain available, with all forms of leave suspended. Hospitals were also told to recall employees who were already on leave.The measures were issued ahead of PTI’s planned September 27 march, which the party says is intended to demand Khan’s release.The preparations have already affected patients. People familiar with the situation told Drop Site that patients scheduled for surgery on Monday were informed that their procedures would be postponed.The government has not publicly said that the hospital preparations are specifically linked to a crackdown on PTI protesters. The documents, however, explicitly refer to preparations for a potential “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident”.The hospital preparations also came as authorities detained Khan’s three sisters – Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr Uzma Khan – along with other members of his family, while several PTI leaders and workers were also arrested ahead of the planned march on Islamabad.Eight members of Khan’s family were reportedly detained within 24 hours. The children were later released after several hours, according to Aleema Khan’s son Shershah Khan, while Khan’s sisters remained in custody.Aleema Khan was detained under Section 3 of Pakistan’s Maintenance of Public Order law, with a formal order issued by Lahore’s deputy commissioner authorising her detention for 30 days, according to documents obtained by Drop Site.Similar detention orders circulated for Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan.The arrests came after authorities stepped up action against PTI members ahead of the September 27 mobilisation. PTI has alleged that party offices were raided and elected representatives and workers were detained across the country.The arrests have come amid continuing concerns from Khan’s family and supporters over his health and prison conditions.Khan’s primary healthcare provider, Dr Faisal Sultan, has reportedly not been allowed to visit him for several weeks. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 after his government was removed from office following a no-confidence vote. PTI has continued to demand his release.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), plans to march on Islamabad on September 27. Hospitals in Islamabad have been ordered to prepare for a possible ‘humanitarian crisis’ and ‘mass casualty incident’ All scheduled elective surgeries have been postponed indefinitely.

Article Title: Pakistan in crisis: PTI to hold Sept 27 stir 'at all costs'; Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders
Article Text:
Pakistan: Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders in court, demand immediate release

PTI says September 27 protest will go ahead

Family condemns detentions

Pakistan's opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will proceed with its planned September 27 protest demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, even as legal challenges have been filed against the preventive detention of his three sisters.A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, according to a report by Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune, as cited by news agency ANI.The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, son of Aleema Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women.The detention orders were issued by the Lahore deputy commissioner on September 20 under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, ahead of PTI's planned September 27 demonstrations.Aleema Khan was detained earlier, while Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were detained on Monday.The petition alleged that Aleema Khan was intercepted while travelling for personal errands and that there was no public gathering or situation at the time that could pose a threat to public order. It also stated that Aleema Khan and her driver, Muhammad Ameer, were being held at Lahore Central Jail.The petitioner described Aleema Khan as a law-abiding individual and alleged that the detention order did not contain specific allegations justifying preventive detention.The respondents named in the petition include the home department secretary, Lahore deputy commissioner, capital city police officer and Lahore Central Jail superintendent, according to The Express Tribune.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi said on Monday that PTI would go ahead with its September 27 protest “at all costs”. He said the party would announce its detailed protest plan on September 25 and mobilise workers across Pakistan.Afridi said arrests of PTI provincial ministers and lawmakers had begun ahead of the protest, prompting an emergency meeting of the party's parliamentary group.He said the party had pursued “all constitutional and democratic avenues” but was being prevented from meeting Imran Khan despite court orders.Afridi said PTI had no intention of confrontation and would pursue its demands through peaceful and democratic means. He also said party workers would not carry weapons during the protest.PTI chairman Barrister Gohar said the party was not planning to “storm” Islamabad and would not take the law and order situation into its own hands. He said the authorities were provoking the party but PTI would not come to Islamabad “like terrorists”.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, said the government would not allow the September 27 protest to disrupt Islamabad. Speaking to reporters in Lahore on Monday, he said preparations were under way for an “assault” and that the government would not allow the capital to be shut down.Imran Khan's son, Kasim Khan, also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.In a post on X, he said, “This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated.”He added, “No news has been released as to where they have been taken. This is criminal behaviour. Inexcusable. The Pakistani people are petrified of their own leaders. No upstanding nation should tolerate this criminal establishment. Intervention is now imperative. The world MUST take action.”The arrests come as PTI prepares for the September 27 protest seeking the release of Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 and is currently held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.
Article Summary: A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi. The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.

Article Title: 'PTI's drama will never achieve anything': Pak minister Naqvi warns Imran Khan's party ahead of Islamabad march
Article Text:
Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI

Also Read:

(With agency inputs)

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday warned jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ahead of the party’s planned protest in Islamabad, saying it “can never achieve anything through such drama. "The PTI plans to march towards the capital on September 27 to demand the release of its founder Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 after being arrested following his conviction in a corruption case. Currently, the cricketer-turned-politician is lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.“We will not allow PTI to enter Islamabad and shut down the city for several days. We have clearly told them that they can never achieve anything through such drama, and I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation,” Naqvi told reporters.He also referred to an Islamabad high court order directing the federal government to ensure peace in the capital and claimed that a majority of PTI leaders did not support the planned protest.“Do not harm yourself and your workers,” he told the PTI leadership, urging it to adopt a “different approach”.Asked about measures to find a long-term solution to the PTI’s repeated protests, Naqvi replied, “This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway.We can't afford this every time.”On reports of a possible ban on the party, he said the government would seek a “once-and-for-all solution.”Meanwhile, the federal government was stepping up security measures ahead of the protest, including placing shipping containers along roads and bringing in police personnel from other provinces.More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, were to be deployed in Islamabad, while more than 30,000 were to be stationed in Attock district, which connects Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Punjab.Police in Rawalpindi, Islamabad’s twin city, have separately sought 9,000 additional personnel to assist the local administration.The PTI is not the only group planning protests in Islamabad. Right-wing Jamaat-e-Islami launched a demonstration against rising petroleum prices on Sunday and was heading towards the capital from Karachi.The Kissan Ittehad farmers’ group has also announced a sit-in in the city this week, seeking relief for farmers.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI ahead of planned protest in Islamabad. Interior minister says party "can never achieve anything through such drama" Federal government stepping up security measures ahead of the protest. More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, to be deployed.

Article Title: 'Broke into house, forced them into vehicles': Imran Khan’s son alleges aunts, cousins 'abducted' in Pakistan
Article Text:
Pakistani Police has already arrested ex-PM Imran Khan's sister in Lahore ahead of party's planned march. (Reuters photo)

More relatives allegedly detained

Aleema's detention ahead of PTI march

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the recent detentions of PTI members are politically motivated? Yes, definitely No, they're justified 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Days before Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march, former prime minister Imran Khan 's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed.In a series of posts on X, Kasim alleged that his aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with cousins Shershah and Shahrez, were taken from their homes after authorities allegedly entered the properties and forced them into vehicles. The claims could not be independently verified.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noureen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez have now been abducted as well,” Kasim said.“They have broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he alleged.Kasim described the alleged detentions as “criminal behaviour” and called for international attention to the matter.Kasim later said the two children of Shahrez, aged four and six, had initially been missing. He subsequently said the children were safe but alleged that two more cousins, Azeem and Sakeenah, had also been taken into custody.“Hearing news that my cousin’s children are now safe. Meanwhile, two more of my cousins have been arrested. Azeem and Sakeenah. No reasons given. No location given,” he said.The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan in Lahore on Sunday. She was ordered to be held for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, with the authorities citing public safety and order concerns. She was later taken to Kot Lakhpat jail, according to police and Pakistani media reports.Lahore deputy commissioner Muhammad Ali Ijaz issued the detention order under the MPO law. The order cited allegations involving protests, roadblocks and the mobilisation of PTI workers.PTI chairman barrister Gohar Ali Khan condemned Aleema's detention and demanded her release, arguing that it could further increase tensions ahead of the September 27 demonstration.Aleema's son Shahrez had earlier alleged that his mother was “abducted” after leaving her home and said the family had no information about where she had been taken.The PTI march is being organised to demand the release of Imran Khan, who remains in jail and is facing multiple legal cases. Pakistani authorities have stepped up measures against PTI supporters ahead of the planned protest.Meanwhile, Pakistani media have reported that Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up in jail amid continuing concerns raised by his family over his health.The government has cited public-order concerns in relation to Aleema Khan's detention, while PTI and members of Imran Khan's family have disputed the action and demanded information about those taken into custody.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed. The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan on Sunday.

Article Title: Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan: 3 killed, several injured as conflict fears grow
Article Text:
Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along border. (AP photo/ File)

Taliban warns of 'crushing response'

Kabul denies sheltering TTP

Afghanistan keeps door open for talks

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the main focus for Pakistan and Afghanistan in resolving their issues? Diplomatic negotiations Border security Intelligence sharing Ceasing cross-border operations 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least three people were killed and several others injured in a Pakistani airstrike targeting Afghanistan's northeastern Kunar province, Tolo News reported on Monday, citing a provincial official.The military strike is supposedly in retaliation for suicide bombing at a police station compound in northwestern Pakistan, raising fears that tensions between the neighbouring nations could once again turn into open fighting.Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February. The latest escalation comes days after the Taliban warned that it would defend Afghan territory against any Pakistani military action.Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, ahead of the imminent Pakistani strikes, had warned Islamabad against carrying out strikes inside Afghanistan, saying Kabul would respond militarily if its territory is attacked.In an interview with Al Arabiya English, Mujahid rejected Pakistan's allegations that militant groups based in Afghanistan recruit, train and launch attacks against Pakistan.“If Pakistan invokes Article 51 to violate the sanctity of Afghan territory, Afghanistan has the right to defend its country, and we will do so,” Mujahid said.He said any Pakistani military operation inside Afghanistan would amount to a violation of Afghan sovereignty and could trigger a strong response from Kabul.Mujahid was responding to comments by a Pakistani military spokesperson, who had told Al Arabiya English that militant groups were using Afghan territory to recruit, train and arm fighters before sending them into Pakistan.Mujahid rejected those allegations and said the Taliban administration does not allow the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan , or TTP, to operate from Afghan soil.He also denied that the Taliban government supports armed groups carrying out attacks against other countries. Instead, Mujahid said Pakistan should examine its own internal security problems, arguing that violence involving the TTP and Baloch armed groups existed before the Taliban returned to power in 2021.Pakistan has repeatedly accused militant groups of operating from Afghanistan and has pressed Kabul to take action against them. The Taliban has consistently denied allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.Despite his warning of military retaliation, Mujahid said Kabul was still willing to engage with Islamabad through dialogue.He called for stronger intelligence-sharing arrangements and greater bilateral cooperation to address security concerns along the two countries' border.Mujahid also backed a possible mediation role for Saudi Arabia, saying Riyadh has good relations with both Afghanistan and Pakistan and could help the two sides resolve their differences.Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along their shared border. The latest airstrike, coming amid fresh security concerns, risks further worsening those ties and could lead to another confrontation between the neighbours.
Article Summary: Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February. The latest escalation comes days after the Taliban warned that it would defend Afghan territory against any Pakistani military action. Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along their shared border.

Article Title: Pakistan braces for protests as govt warns of $400 million daily loss
Article Text:
Protests in Pakistan (Representative image)

Government warns of economic fallout

Islamabad steps up security

Pakistan’s government has put heavy restrictions on protestors warning them that those seeking to march towards Islamabad with the government warning that disruptions could cost the economy around $400 million a day as separate marches by Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital.Pakistan’s information minister Attaullah Tarar said on Sunday that the administration, police and interior ministry were clear that groups intending to cause disruption would not be allowed to reach the capital. He cited a recent Islamabad high court ruling that bars political parties from obstructing public roads and the movement of citizens.The warning comes ahead of a PTI nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad on September 27 seeking the release of party founder Imran Khan, who is incarcerated. JI, meanwhile, has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital.Pakistan’s finance minister Muhammad Aurangzeb separately warned that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan’s economy every day.According to estimates prepared by the planning commission and finance ministry, the services sector, including financial services, communication, retail, transport, wholesale and hospitality, could account for about PKR 86 billion of the daily loss.Industry could lose PKR 25 billion and agriculture PKR 9 billion, while the government could face an additional revenue loss of around PKR 17 billion.Aurangzeb said the disruption would come at a time when businesses were already dealing with higher freight and insurance costs and supply-chain problems linked to tensions in the Middle East, including disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.He also warned about the impact on IT exports. Pakistan recorded $811 million in IT exports during July and August, he said, adding that previous internet disruptions during episodes of civil disobedience had affected IT exports by as much as 80%.Authorities have begun preparing for the potential marches, with hundreds of containers placed at entry points to Islamabad. Police officials have also reviewed security arrangements at major entry and exit points and other sensitive locations.The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and Federal Government Polyclinic Hospital have been placed on high alert, with emergency, trauma, ICU, operating theatre, blood bank and ambulance services instructed to remain fully operational. Pims said the arrangements would remain in place until September 30.The government has also cited concerns over statements by PTI leaders about the planned march. Pakistan’s parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said a reported remark by a senior PTI leader about turning Islamabad into “Somnath” had raised concerns about possible violence. He said the government had a responsibility to maintain law and order in the capital.The government has said it remains in contact with JI leadership and hopes to resolve the dispute through dialogue. JI has been protesting since August 16 against the petroleum levy and says it wants the government to withdraw the levy.
Article Summary: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek- i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital. JI has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital. Government warns that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan's economy every day.

Article Title: Jailed former Pak PM Imran Khan undergoes medical check-up amid concerns over health
Article Text:
Imran Khan

Geo News

Jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up at Adiala Jail amid concerns over his health, according to a media report on Sunday.Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 following his conviction in a corruption case and is currently lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.According to, a specialist team from the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) examined Khan at the jail. The check-up included assessments of his blood pressure, cholesterol levels and eyesight.The medical team was led by a PIMS doctor, with medical staff from the Adiala Jail hospital assisting during the examination, the report said.Khan has previously complained of an eye condition and has been taken to PIMS several times for treatment. His supporters have alleged that his health has deteriorated due to inadequate medical care, a claim that prison authorities have repeatedly rejected.The Supreme Court had ordered on August 18 that Khan be shifted to a private medical facility for treatment. However, he was taken to PIMS, where he underwent medical tests before being returned to jail, news agency ANI cited.His Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has sought his transfer to Islamabad's Shifa International Hospital for a detailed medical examination and treatment, while raising concerns over his health.The party has also announced a September 27 demonstration seeking Khan's release.Khan has faced multiple legal cases since his removal as prime minister through a no-confidence vote in April 2022, with his health and conditions of detention remaining a recurring issue in Pakistan's political discourse.
Article Summary: Imran Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 following his conviction in a corruption case. Khan has previously complained of an eye condition and has been taken to PIMS several times for treatment. His supporters have alleged that his health has deteriorated due to inadequate medical care.

Article Title: Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan's sister Aleema arrested in Lahore ahead of Sept 27 PTI march
Article Text:
Aleema Khan arrested ahead of planned Imran Khan-founded PTI march

Long-imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan 's sister, Aleema Khan, was arrested from her home in Lahore on Sunday ahead of a planned march on September 27.Police arrested Aleema as she was planning a protest march organised by Imran Khan-founded Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). A PTI spokesperson confirmed her arrest to Reuters.A notification issued by Lahore's district administration said Aleema Khan had been arrested and sent to jail for 30 days, citing concerns over public safety.“According to intelligence reports, her presence at any public place will pose a grave threat to public safety,” the notification said.Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has planned a march to Islamabad next week, demanding the former prime minister's release.Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Saturday that the government would take all possible measures to prevent the protest march.Zulfi Bukhari, a close aide to Imran Khan, condemned Aleema's arrest as “absolutely despicable”.“The fear of the 27th protest is clearly taking its toll,” Bukhari said.The World Cup-winning cricket captain and former prime minister Imran Khan has been imprisoned for more than three years.Khan's family, including his two sons, have repeatedly expressed concern over his health and alleged a conspiracy involving Pakistan's de facto leader and military chief Asim Munir.
Article Summary: Aleema Khan arrested ahead of planned Imran Khan-founded PTI march. Imran Khan's sister sent to jail for 30 days, citing concerns over public safety. Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has planned a march to Islamabad next week.

Article Title: Pakistan foreign minister dials Iranian counterpart, urges uninterrupted energy supplies and safe passage of ships
Article Text:
Abbas Araghchi and Ishaq Dar (File photo)

(With PTI inputs)

Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure “uninterrupted energy supplies” and the “safe and expeditious passage of ships”, amid concerns over disruptions to crucial waterways in the Middle East.Dar, who also serves as Pakistan’s deputy prime minister, held a telephonic conversation with Araghchi to discuss the latest regional developments, according to a statement from Pakistan’s Foreign Office (FO) on X.During the call, Dar “stressed the importance of uninterrupted energy supplies and the safe and expeditious passage of ships, particularly given their implications for developing countries and global supply chains”.He also underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region”, the FO noted.The two ministers agreed to maintain close cooperation and meet in New York City next week on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, the foreign office added.The conversation came amid growing concerns over the safety of oil supply routes as tensions escalate around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, as well as uncertainty surrounding the United States-Iran war, which began on February 28.The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, while Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.The Strait of Hormuz has been under a virtual Iranian blockade since March, with Tehran effectively restricting passage through the critical maritime corridor in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks on Iran that triggered the conflict.Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi forces, aligned with Tehran, have imposed a de facto blockade on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait since July, seizing key shoreline territory and Mayun Island while specifically targeting Saudi-linked shipping and energy infrastructure.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure ‘uninterrupted energy supplies’ Dar also underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region’

Article Title: 'We want to go home': Hindu minor sisters abducted, converted, married in Pakistan's Sindh
Article Text:
Pakistan: Two minor Hindu sisters allegedly abducted, converted and forced into marriage

Sindh at centre of concern over minority girls

The alleged abduction and forced conversion of two minor Hindu sisters in Pakistan's Sindh province has triggered fresh concern among minority rights group, with one organisation calling for an independent probe and safeguards for the girls.According to Voice of Pakistan Minority, Roopi, 13 and Seeta, 14, were allegedly taken from Ibrahim Colony in Tando Allahyar district and later converted to Islam and married to two Muslim men, Amjad Solangi and Mansood Solangi.The sisters were subsequently brought before a court in Tando Allahyar in an abduction case. Instead of sending them back to their family, the court placed them in a safe house, VOPM said.The rights group said the girls appeared distressed outside the court and were heard pleading to be taken home. A video circulating online also purportedly showed the sisters saying, “Let us go to our parents” and “We want to go home.”VOPM said the circumstances surrounding the case made it important that the sisters be heard independently, without anyone who could influence or intimidate them.“The state must interview Roopi and Seeta in a child-sensitive environment, away from alleged husbands, religious figures, intermediaries or anyone who could pressure them.Officials must allow the girls to speak freely and must provide them independent legal support and protection,” VOPM said.The organisation called for an urgent, independent and transparent investigation into the allegations.The case has also renewed attention on the vulnerability of Hindu families in Sindh, which has Pakistan's largest Hindu population.
